He appears confused and agitated. Vitals are as follows: BP 90/40, HR 120 bpm, and RR 20. Which variable should be monitored as a good indicator of prognosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 37-year-old man is admitted for septic shock secondary to cellulitis. He is started on IV fluids and broad-spectrum antibiotics after blood cultures are sent. He appears confused and agitated. Vitals are as follows: BP 90/40, HR 120 bpm, and RR 20. Which variable should be monitored as a good indicator of prognosis?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Lactate: Lactate levels can be monitored to assess hypoperfusion and prognosis. Shock is characterized by inadequate tissue perfusion, leading to increased anaerobic metabolism and lactic acidosis production. This increase in lactate may be buffered at first, so ABG may not reflect this change in PH in early shock. Lactate can be used as a marker for tissue hypoperfusion, and a serum level >4 mmol/L strongly correlates with sepsis. Lactate clearance correlates with improved tissue perfusion. As lactate levels increase from 2 to 8 mmol/L, mortality rates also increase from 10-90%. Higher lactate clearance is associated with better prognosis and outcomes. Incorrect Options: Option A - Arterial blood gas (ABG): ABG is a valuable tool for assessing a patient's acid-base status and oxygenation. In the context of septic shock, it can provide information about the patient's pH, partial pressure of oxygen (PaO2), partial pressure of carbon dioxide (PaCO2), bicarbonate (HCO3-), and oxygen saturation (SaO2). However, while ABG can show changes in pH related to acidosis, it may not accurately reflect the rise in lactate levels in early shock. Lactate levels can increase before significant changes in pH are evident in the blood gas analysis. Therefore, while ABG is essential for assessing acid-base homeostasis, it may not be the most reliable indicator of prognosis in septic shock. Option B - Brain natriuretic peptide (BNP): Brain natriuretic peptide is a hormone secreted by the heart in response to increased pressure and volume in the cardiac chambers. Elevated BNP levels are associated with heart failure and can be helpful in diagnosing and assessing the severity of cardiogenic shock. However, in the case of septic shock secondary to cellulitis, the primary cause of shock is not cardiogenic, and therefore, monitoring BNP levels may not provide relevant information about the prognosis of septic shock in this patient. Option D - Complete blood count (CBC): A complete blood count provides valuable information about the patient's red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. In the context of septic shock, the CBC can help identify an underlying infection if the white blood cell count (WBC) is elevated. Additionally, the platelet count may be low in the setting of coagulopathy and sepsis. While CBC is essential for assessing the patient's overall health and identifying potential complications related to infection and coagulation, it may not directly reflect the degree of tissue hypoperfusion and prognosis in septic shock. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option A - Group A beta-hemolytic streptococcus and Staphylococcus aureus: The patient's presentation with ill-defined erythema and tenderness progressing rapidly to indurated, dusky, and necrotic skin with bullae and an exudative, malodorous discharge, along with the presence of palpable crepitus, is characteristic of necrotizing fasciitis. Necrotizing fasciitis is a severe soft tissue infection that involves the rapid destruction of fascial planes and surrounding tissues. It is a life-threatening condition that requires immediate and aggressive treatment. Group A beta-hemolytic streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes) and Staphylococcus aureus are the most common pathogens responsible for necrotizing fasciitis. These bacteria produce enzymes and toxins that facilitate the rapid spread of infection and tissue destruction. The infection can progress rapidly, leading to sepsis, shock, and organ failure if not treated promptly. It is not a common cause of necrotizing fasciitis. Option D - Streptococcus bovis: it is a bacterium that has been associated with infective endocarditis, especially in patients with colorectal cancer. questions.answerText: The first hour of recognition of septic shock
questions.solution: Correct Option A - The first hour of recognition of septic shock: The administration of effective intravenous antimicrobials within the first hour of recognition of septic shock (grade 1B) and severe sepsis without septic shock should be the goal of therapy. Although most evidence supports the prompt administration of antibiotics following the recognition of severe sepsis and septic shock, the feasibility with which clinicians may achieve this ideal state has not been scientifically evaluated. Moreover, initial empiric anti-infective therapy should include 1 or more drugs that have activity against all likely pathogens (bacterial and/or fungal or viral) and that penetrate in adequate concentrations into the tissues presumed to be the source of sepsis. The antimicrobial regimen should be reassessed daily for potential de-escalation to prevent the development of resistance, reduce toxicity, and reduce costs. It is suggested to use low procalcitonin levels or similar biomarkers to aid the discontinuation of empiric antibiotics in patients who appeared septic but had no subsequent evidence of infection. Incorrect Options: Option B - First 2 hours of recognition of septic shock: Although the feasibility of a one-hour target for initiating antibiotics has not been tested, the rationale for using it is based on observational studies that show poor outcomes with delayed (even beyond one hour), inadequately dosed, or inappropriate (ie, treatment with antibiotics to which the pathogen was later shown to be in vitro resistant) antimicrobial therapy. questions.stem: A 40-year-old patient with a medical history pertinent for acquired immunodeficiency virus presents with complaints of blurring in his central vision and increased floaters in the right eye. After a dilated ophthalmic examination, the patient is diagnosed with cytomegalovirus retinitis. Induction treatment with foscarnet is initiated. Which of the following laboratory studies should be followed closely during and after this patient’s treatment?
questions.stemHtml:
A 40-year-old patient with a medical history pertinent for acquired immunodeficiency virus presents with complaints of blurring in his central vision and increased floaters in the right eye. After a dilated ophthalmic examination, the patient is diagnosed with cytomegalovirus retinitis. Induction treatment with foscarnet is initiated.
Which of the following laboratory studies should be followed closely during and after this patient’s treatment?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Serum creatinine level: Foscarnet is an antiviral agent that is indicated for use only in immunocompromised patients who develop severe viral infections (e.g. cytomegalovirus retinitis). The major toxicity associated with the use of foscarnet is renal impairment . As such, serum creatinine should be followed closely. Foscarnet is an inhibitor of many viral RNA and DNA polymerases. The majority of patients treated with foscarnet will experience at least some degree of renal impairment during treatment. Most commonly, renal impairment is reversible with dose adjustments or discontinuation of therapy. To help reduce the risk of nephrotoxicity, remember to calculate the creatinine clearance even if serum creatinine remains in the normal range so that any necessary dose adjustments can be made. Electrolyte imbalances including hypocalcemia, hyper/hypophosphatemia, hypomagnesemia, or hypokalemia are possible. Significant imbalances, if present, can cause seizures. Incorrect Options: Option A - Alanine aminotransferase: Treatment with foscarnet is not typically associated with hepatotoxicity. Thus, monitoring LFT is imperative. Option C - Brain natriuretic peptide: In patients with coexisting heart failure, it may be necessary to monitor volume status with the brain natriuretic peptide. Foscarnet should be used with caution in patients with renal failure. Option D - Alkaline phosphatase: It is not routinely necessary to follow the alkaline phosphatase level when treating a patient with foscarnet. @Neet_pg_bot

The patient also recalls experiencing recurrent pneumonia since childhood. On further questioning, the patient mentions occasional oral candidiasis but denies any family history of similar symptoms. Physical examination reveals no notable findings. Laboratory tests show reduced levels of serum IgA, while the levels of other immunoglobulins are within the normal range. Which primary immunodeficiency disorder is the most likely cause of the patient's symptoms and laboratory findings?

Which primary immunodeficiency disorder is the most likely cause of the patient's symptoms and laboratory findings?
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Selective IgA Deficiency: Selective IgA Deficiency is the most likely cause of the patient's symptoms and laboratory findings. This disorder is characterized by a deficiency of serum IgA, while the levels of other immunoglobulins are usually within the normal range. Patients with selective IgA deficiency are often asymptomatic, but they can present with recurrent infections, particularly in the respiratory and gastrointestinal tracts. Additionally, they may experience other complications like allergies and autoimmune disorders. The patient's history of frequent episodes of diarrhea, recurrent pneumonia, and oral candidiasis, along with the reduced IgA levels, are indicative of selective IgA deficiency. Incorrect Options: Option A - X-Linked Agammaglobulinemia (XLA): X-Linked Agammaglobulinemia is a primary immunodeficiency disorder characterized by a deficiency in B cells, leading to a lack of immunoglobulins (antibodies) of all classes. Patients with XLA typically present with recurrent bacterial infections, particularly in the respiratory tract. This disorder is more common in males and is caused by mutations in the Bruton's tyrosine kinase (BTK) gene. Option B - Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID): SCID refers to a group of rare and severe primary immunodeficiency disorders where both the cellular and humoral arms of the immune system are impaired. Patients with SCID are highly susceptible to severe, life-threatening infections. They often present early in life with recurrent and opportunistic infections. SCID is usually caused by genetic defects affecting multiple immune components. Option C - Common Variable Immunodeficiency (CVID): Common Variable Immunodeficiency is characterized by low levels of immunoglobulins, particularly IgG and IgA, resulting in recurrent bacterial infections, particularly in the respiratory and gastrointestinal tracts. However, this disorder does not typically present with isolated IgA deficiency, and reduced levels of serum IgA alone are not the hallmark feature of CVID. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A newborn infant is brought to the clinic by his parents due to recurrent and severe infections. The child appears healthy at birth but starts experiencing various infections shortly after. The child has chronic diarrhea and is failing to thrive. Physical examination reveals absent lymph nodes and tonsils. Laboratory tests show absence of T cells, B cells, and NK cells. Thymic shadow is also absent on imaging. Which of the following conditions is the most likely cause of these clinical findings?
questions.stemHtml: A newborn infant is brought to the clinic by his parents due to recurrent and severe infections. The child appears healthy at birth but starts experiencing various infections shortly after. The child has chronic diarrhea and is failing to thrive. Which of the following conditions is the most likely cause of these clinical findings?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID): Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID) is a group of rare, genetic disorders that result in a severe impairment of both cellular and humoral immunity. This means that both T cells and B cells are affected, leading to an inability to fight off infections. The absence of T cells, B cells, NK cells, and a thymic shadow on imaging strongly indicates SCID. There are several genetic causes of SCID, including mutations in genes involved in lymphocyte development and function. Incorrect Options: Option A - Hyper IgM Syndrome: Hyper IgM Syndrome is a primary immunodeficiency disorder characterized by the inability of B cells to switch from producing IgM antibodies to other antibody classes (IgG, IgA, IgE), leading to elevated IgM levels and decreased levels of other antibody classes. It is typically caused by mutations in the CD40 ligand gene. While infections are common in Hyper IgM Syndrome, the absence of T cells, B cells, and NK cells, along with the absent thymic shadow, points towards a more severe immunodeficiency condition than Hyper IgM Syndrome. Option B - Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome: Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome is an X-linked primary immunodeficiency disorder caused by mutations in the WAS gene, leading to defects in platelet function and immune cell signaling. It is characterized by thrombocytopenia (low platelet count), eczema, and recurrent infections. While it can lead to immune dysfunction, the absence of T cells, B cells, and NK cells, along with the absent thymic shadow, suggests a more profound immunodeficiency than Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome. Option D - Ataxia-Telangiectasia: Ataxia-Telangiectasia is a rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the ATM gene. It primarily affects the nervous system, leading to symptoms like progressive ataxia (lack of muscle control), telangiectasia (dilated blood vessels), and an increased risk of certain cancers. While Ataxia-Telangiectasia can also result in immune system dysfunction, the absence of lymph nodes, tonsils, and thymic shadow on imaging suggests a more profound immunodeficiency than what is typically seen in Ataxia-Telangiectasia. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: A 6-year-old boy presents with recurrent infections, particularly respiratory infections. His parents report that he has never had any severe infections, but he seems to catch colds frequently. Physical examination reveals that he has normal-sized lymph nodes and spleen. However, his tonsils appear small. Laboratory tests show a normal T cell count and reduced levels of all immunoglobulin classes. Which stage of B cell development involves positive and negative selection processes that determine the functionality of B cell receptors?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Immature B cell stage: At this stage, the B cell has successfully rearranged both heavy and light chain genes to form a functional BCR. However, the BCR is not yet fully mature and self-tolerant. The immature B cell undergoes positive and negative selection processes in the bone marrow and spleen. Positive selection ensures that the BCR can interact with antigens, while negative selection eliminates B cells with strongly self-reactive BCRs to prevent autoimmunity. Incorrect Options: Option A - Early Pre-B cell stage: This stage occurs in the bone marrow, where B cell progenitors undergo rearrangement of their immunoglobulin heavy chain genes. This process leads to the formation of a functional μ (mu) heavy chain protein. However, there is no direct involvement of positive or negative selection processes in this stage. Option B - Late Pre-B cell stage: In this stage, the B cell precursor completes rearrangement of the immunoglobulin heavy chain genes and forms a pre-BCR complex with a surrogate light chain. This complex signals to the developing B cell that the heavy chain is functional. Again, there is no direct involvement of positive or negative selection processes in this stage. Option D - Mature B cell stage: B cells that have successfully passed through the positive and negative selection processes become mature B cells. They leave the bone marrow and migrate to secondary lymphoid organs (such as lymph nodes and spleen) where they can encounter antigens and participate in immune responses. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option D - Gaucher disease: Gaucher disease is a rare genetic disorder caused by the deficiency of an enzyme called glucocerebrosidase, leading to the accumulation of a substance called glucocerebroside in cells, particularly macrophages. Laboratory findings in rheumatoid arthritis are more focused on autoimmune markers and inflammatory markers rather than anemia and thrombocytopenia. questions.stem: A 38-year-old female, otherwise in good health, was driving with relatives when their vehicle got stuck in the sand. Later, the relatives found her unresponsive in the van. As she was pulled out, a strong smell of fumes was noticed. The paramedics noticed agitation and intubated her in the field. In less than 2 hours, the patient is taken to the ER of the nearby hospital. The oxygen saturation as measured by pulse oximeter is 100% on 100 percent oxygen. She is sedated. Her temperature is 98.0°F, pulse is 88/min, and BP is 121/86 mm of Hg. A co-oximeter measured carboxyhemoglobin (CO-Hb) level is 26%, and hyperbaric oxygen (HBO) therapy is considered. Which biochemical measurement is suggested as a marker of severity of poisoning?
questions.stemHtml: A 38-year-old female, otherwise in good health, was driving with relatives when their vehicle got stuck in the sand. Later, the relatives found her unresponsive in the van. As she was pulled out, a strong smell of fumes was noticed. The paramedics noticed agitation and intubated her in the field. Her temperature is 98.0°F, pulse is 88/min, and BP is 121/86 mm of Hg. A co-oximeter measured carboxyhemoglobin (CO-Hb) level is 26%, and hyperbaric oxygen (HBO) therapy is considered. Which biochemical measurement is suggested as a marker of severity of poisoning?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Lactate: CO-Hgb levels are likely positively correlated with initial lactate levels in carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning. Patients who received HBO treatment had elevated plasma lactate concentrations and additionally had more frequent altered mental status. Although HBO therapy is used in different settings, generally accepted indications for HBO treatment are the presence of significantly increased COHb values and neurologic or cardiac deterioration. However, a lactate value >1.85mmol/L can predict the need for HBO treatment, which could be taken as a measure of severe poisoning. Lactate levels are also increased in alcohol intoxication, salicylate poisoning, and paraquat poisoning. Incorrect Options: Option B - Carboxyhemoglobin (CO-Hgb): While carboxyhemoglobin levels are measured to confirm carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning and guide treatment decisions, it is not considered a marker of the severity of poisoning. CO-Hgb levels indicate the percentage of hemoglobin that is bound to carbon monoxide instead of oxygen. A high CO-Hgb level, as in this case (26%), confirms the diagnosis of CO poisoning, but it does not provide information about the severity of the poisoning or the degree of tissue hypoxia. The severity of CO poisoning is better assessed by clinical features, such as the patient's mental status, oxygen saturation, and the presence of symptoms like confusion, agitation, or altered consciousness. Option C - Creatinine: Creatinine levels are not used as a marker of severity in carbon monoxide poisoning. Creatinine is a waste product produced by muscles and excreted by the kidneys. It is commonly measured to assess kidney function and to estimate glomerular filtration rate (GFR). In cases of carbon monoxide poisoning, the focus is on assessing the extent of tissue hypoxia and damage caused by the lack of oxygen, rather than kidney function. Option D - Creatine phosphokinase (CrPK or CPK): Creatine phosphokinase (also known as creatine kinase or CPK) is an enzyme found in various tissues, including muscle and brain cells. Elevated CPK levels can indicate muscle damage, such as in muscle injuries, heart attacks, or rhabdomyolysis. However, CPK levels are not used as a marker of severity in carbon monoxide poisoning. The focus in CO poisoning is primarily on evaluating the extent of tissue hypoxia and its effects on the brain and other organs @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which of the following best characterizes restrictive lung diseases, such as pulmonary fibrosis?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following best characterizes restrictive lung diseases, such as pulmonary fibrosis?

options.label: A
options.text: Both FEV and FVC are reduced, but characteristically the FEV1.0/FVC% is normal or increased

options.label: B
options.text: The FEV1.0 is reduced much more than the FVC, giving a low FEV/FVC%

options.label: C
options.text: Reduction of the forced expiratory flow rate, or FEF 25-75%

options.label: D
options.text: The total lung capacity is increased to about 120%

questions.answerText: Both FEV and FVC are reduced, but characteristically the FEV1.0/FVC% is normal or increased
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Both FEV and FVC are reduced, but characteristically the FEV1.0/FVC% is normal or increased: In restrictive lung disease, such as pulmonary fibrosis, both FEV and FVC are reduced, but characteristically the FEV1.0/FVC% is normal or increased. Additional characteristics of restrictive lung disease include a total lung capacity which will be around 4 L or less. Incorrect Options: Option B - The FEV 1.0 is reduced much more than the FVC, giving a low FEV/FVC%: This characteristic is typical of obstructive lung diseases, not restrictive lung diseases like pulmonary fibrosis. In obstructive lung diseases, such as bronchial asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), the airways are narrowed, leading to increased resistance to airflow. This results in a greater reduction in the forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1.0) compared to the forced vital capacity (FVC). As a result, the FEV1.0/FVC% ratio is reduced, often below the normal range. Option C - Reduction of the forced expiratory flow rate, or FEF 25-75%: The reduction of the forced expiratory flow rate between 25% and 75% of the FVC (FEF25-75%) is not a characteristic feature of restrictive lung diseases like pulmonary fibrosis. Instead, it is more commonly seen in obstructive lung diseases, where there is narrowing of the airways and reduced flow rates during the mid-portion of forced expiration. It can be an early indicator of early-stage COPD before other lung function indicators, such as FEV1.0, become abnormal. Option D - The total lung capacity is increased to about 120%: An increased total lung capacity to about 120% (around 6 liters) is a characteristic finding in obstructive lung diseases, not in restrictive lung diseases. In obstructive lung diseases, the increased total lung capacity is due to air trapping caused by difficulty in fully exhaling air from the lungs, leading to a higher volume of air remaining in the lungs after exhalation. In restrictive lung diseases, like pulmonary fibrosis, the total lung capacity is reduced to around 4 liters or less due to the limited expansion of the lungs caused by the fibrotic changes in the lung tissue. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: What is the most appropriate strategy to address “never” events (like cutting off the wrong limb in surgery or performing CPR on a DNR patient)?
questions.stemHtml: What is the most appropriate strategy to address “never” events (like cutting off the wrong limb in surgery or performing CPR on a DNR patient)?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Provide greater transparency: Providing greater transparency is the most appropriate strategy to address "never" events, which are serious medical errors that should never occur and can lead to severe harm or even death of a patient. Transparency involves openly sharing information about the event with all relevant stakeholders, including patients, families, healthcare providers, and hospital administrators. This transparency allows for a thorough and honest investigation of the event to understand the root causes and contributing factors. By openly discussing and analyzing the event, healthcare organizations can identify areas of improvement and implement changes to prevent similar incidents in the future. Transparency also helps build trust between patients and healthcare providers, as patients feel more informed and involved in their care. Incorrect Options: Option A - Report to supervising agency: Reporting the "never" event to a supervising agency, such as a regulatory body or accreditation organization, is an essential step to ensure that the incident is appropriately documented and investigated. However, this action alone may not be sufficient to address the underlying issues and prevent future occurrences. The supervising agency may impose sanctions or penalties, but this does not necessarily lead to process improvement or a culture of safety within the healthcare organization. Option B - Actively re-train medical staff: Re-training medical staff can be a valuable response if improper training contributed to the "never" event. However, "never" events are often the result of systemic failures rather than individual errors. He denies fevers, coughing, chest pain or pressure, palpitations, orthopnea, and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea. Cardiovascular examination is unremarkable. There is no jugular venous distention or lower extremity edema. Pulmonary examination is unremarkable. He is a nonsmoker and a retired roofer. Which of the following statements concerning asbestos-induced lung disease is accurate?

questions.answerText: Asbestos exposure increases the risk of lung cancer associated with cigarette smoke exposure
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Asbestos exposure increases the risk of lung cancer associated with cigarette smoke exposure: The risk of lung cancer associated with exposure to both asbestos and cigarette smoke appears to be multiplicative. A 1979 report in the Annals of the New York Academy of Science showed that asbestos is associated with a 6-fold increase, cigarette smoking with an 11-fold increase, and both cigarette smoke and asbestos exposure with a 59-fold increase in the risk of lung cancer. Incorrect Options: Option B - Coughing, sputum production, and wheezing are the most common presenting symptoms: Coughing, sputum production, and wheezing are not the most common presenting symptoms of asbestos-induced lung disease. The most common presenting symptom of asbestos-induced lung disease is dyspnea, which can be a result of interstitial lung disease (asbestosis) or lung cancer. Asbestos exposure primarily affects the lungs' interstitium, leading to fibrosis and scarring, which can cause progressive dyspnea. Option C - Antinuclear antibody, rheumatoid factor, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate have prognostic implications : Antinuclear antibody (ANA), rheumatoid factor (RF), and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) are not specific markers for asbestos-induced lung disease. These are nonspecific laboratory tests and are not used for diagnosing or prognosticating asbestos-related lung conditions. Asbestosis and asbestos-related lung diseases are diagnosed based on clinical history, occupational exposure, radiographic findings, and pulmonary function tests. Option D - Cigarette exposure does not increase the risk of lung cancer associated with asbestos exposure : Cigarette exposure does increase the risk of lung cancer associated with asbestos exposure. Both asbestos exposure and cigarette smoking are independent risk factors for the development of lung cancer. When a person is exposed to both asbestos and cigarette smoke, the risk of lung cancer is synergistically increased. As mentioned in the correct answer, the risk of lung cancer associated with exposure to both asbestos and cigarette smoke appears to be multiplicative. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 25-year-old male is admitted to the ER for the management of a severe asthma attack. He is nauseated and complains of vomiting and diarrhea. The patient has a long history of severe asthma with multiple hospitalizations and 1 intubation 5 years ago. He developed shortness of breath 2 days ago that has progressively worsened. He tried at-home albuterol, ipratropium nebulizers, and cromolyn therapy, but nothing improved his symptoms. In the hospital, albuterol is administered continuously, but he fails to improve. His current peak flow rates are decreased by nearly 50% from baseline. Which agent should be added to the patient’s therapy at this time?
questions.stemHtml: A 25-year-old male is admitted to the ER for the management of a severe asthma attack. He is nauseated and complains of vomiting and diarrhea. The patient has a long history of severe asthma with multiple hospitalizations and 1 intubation 5 years ago. He developed shortness of breath 2 days ago that has progressively worsened. He tried at-home albuterol, ipratropium nebulizers, and cromolyn therapy, but nothing improved his symptoms. In the hospital, albuterol is administered continuously, but he fails to improve. His current peak flow rates are decreased by nearly 50% from baseline. Which agent should be added to the patient’s therapy at this time?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Intravenous methylprednisolone: It is most appropriate to add an intravenous steroidal agent, such as hydrocortisone, to augment the action of bronchodilators by reducing inflammation surrounding the airways. Systemic glucocorticoid therapy is indicated for asthma exacerbations that are refractory to intensive bronchodilator therapy due to the persistent airflow obstruction potentially being secondary to airway inflammation and intraluminal mucus plugging. Other indications for systemic glucocorticoids are asthma exacerbations that occurs despite ongoing daily or alternate-day oral glucocorticoid therapy, or in patients who have a recurrent exacerbation after recent discontinuation of systemic glucocorticoids for a previous exacerbation. In general, the efficacy of an oral agent is equal to an intravenous agent in an acute situation. In this case, there is a concern about the absorption of the oral agent due to nausea/vomiting. Incorrect Options: Option A - Inhaled beclomethasone: Is a corticosteroid that is typically used for long-term control of asthma symptoms, but it does not provide immediate relief during an acute exacerbation. This medication works by reducing inflammation and swelling in the airways, but the effects are not instant. In an acute setting, systemic corticosteroids such as methylprednisolone would be more beneficial as they work more rapidly and effectively. Option B - Disodium cromoglycate: (Also known as cromolyn sodium) is a mast cell stabilizer, which works by preventing the release of substances from mast cells that can cause inflammation in the airways. This medication is used prophylactically to prevent asthma attacks, rather than to treat an acute attack. Cromoglycate is typically used in individuals who have a known trigger (e.g., exercise-induced asthma) or in those who have not responded well to other preventive therapies. Option D - Theophylline: Is a bronchodilator that is used to prevent and treat symptoms of asthma and other lung diseases. However, its use has declined due to its narrow therapeutic index and the availability of other more effective and safer treatments. Theophylline can be used in an acute setting, but it's typically reserved for severe cases that are not responsive to other treatments due to its side effect profile and the need for serum level monitoring. In this scenario, the use of a systemic corticosteroid, such as methylprednisolone, would be more effective for treating an acute asthma exacerbation. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man with COPD is brought to the ER with shortness of breath. Upper lung predominant emphysema is not present. He admits to frequent hospitalizations (at least 5 in the past 3 months) for COPD exacerbations. He complains of progressively worsening of shortness of breath and a productive cough with copious amounts of yellow-green sputum. The patient is a lifelong smoker (90 pack-years). Comorbid medical conditions include hypertension, ischemic heart disease, and gastroesophageal reflux disease. He is currently on ipratropium, aspirin, nitroglycerin, hydrochlorothiazide, lisinopril, and omeprazole, in addition to home oxygen at 2 L/min via nasal cannula. The patient's vitals are as follows: temperature 37.4 degrees Celsius (99.4 degrees Fahrenheit), blood pressure 150/90 mmHg, pulse 116/min, and respirations 29/min. A physical examination of the lungs demonstrates decreased breath sounds and wheezing bilaterally. Cardiovascular examination reveals a loud second heart sound. His abdomen is soft, non-tender, and non-distended. His liver is slightly enlarged. Examination of the extremities reveals 3+ lower-extremity edema. Arterial blood gas analysis shows pH 7.35, PO2 53 mmHg, PCO2 59 mmHg, and HCO3 31 mEq/L. The patient is admitted to the medical unit and receives methylprednisolone and azithromycin as part of his treatment regimen. Which of the following has shown the greatest evidence of direct mortality improvement in COPD?

Arterial blood gas analysis shows pH 7.35, PO2 53 mmHg, PCO2 59 mmHg, and HCO3 31 mEq/L. questions.solution: Correct Option B - Oxygen therapy: Oxygen therapy is the only treatment modality that definitively decreases morbidity and mortality significantly in patients with COPD. Criteria for initiation of oxygen therapy include the following: resting PaO 2 <55 mmHg, oxygen saturation <88%, PaO 2 <59 mmHg with evidence of cor pulmonale, erythrocytosis, and hematocrit >55%. The other treatment modalities in the other answer choices do not clearly decrease morbidity and mortality in patients with COPD. Other modalities (which were not answer choices) which have demonstrated (small) mortality benefits include the combination of salmeterol + fluticasone (as per the "TORCH" trial), long-acting beta-agonists (LABA) + inhaled glucocorticoid combinations, and tiotropium + inhaled LABA + inhaled corticosteroid combination, along with possibly pulmonary rehab. Incorrect Options: Option A - Antibiotics: Antibiotics are typically used in acute exacerbations of COPD, especially when there's an indication of bacterial infection, such as increased purulent sputum. However, their use has not been shown to reduce long-term mortality in patients with COPD. They help in managing the acute episode but do not alter the course of the disease. Option C - Corticosteroids: Corticosteroids can be beneficial in the management of acute exacerbations of COPD and may improve symptoms and lung function, but they have not been shown to reduce long-term mortality. In fact, prolonged use of systemic corticosteroids can lead to serious side effects such as osteoporosis, diabetes, and adrenal suppression. Option D - Lung Volume Reduction Surgery (LVRS): This is a surgical intervention where sections of the most damaged parts of the lungs are removed to allow the remaining healthier parts to function more effectively. It is primarily used in selected patients with emphysema and can lead to improvement in lung function and quality of life, but it does not necessarily reduce mortality for all COPD patients. Its utility is limited by surgical risks and specific patient selection criteria. LVRS has been shown to have mortality benefit in a subgroup of patients with upper lobe predominant emphysema and low exercise capacity. The patient in this vignette does not have upper lobe predominant emphysema and therefore would not be a candidate for LVRS. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: A mutation in the JAG1 gene is associated with which of the following congenital conditions affecting the biliary tract?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Alagille syndrome: Alagille syndrome is characterized by a paucity of interlobular bile ducts. Cholestasis, pulmonic stenosis, dysmorphic facies, butterfly vertebrae, and renal dysplasia are also associated with Alagille syndrome. Patients often have short stature and may have developmental delay. Mutations in the JAG1 gene are associated with more than 90% of cases and are transmitted through autosomal dominant inheritance. Cholestatic liver disease severity is variable, and management may range from conservative treatment for symptoms like pruritus to liver transplantation in 20% of patients who develop end-stage renal disease. Incorrect Options: Option A - Caroli disease: Caroli disease is associated with the PKHD1 gene, which is primarily expressed in the kidneys in addition to the liver, pancreas, and lungs. questions.solution: Correct Option D - Increased nucleation of cholesterol: Sludge formation represents an early stage of gallstone formation. It is formed of precipitates of cholesterol and calcium bilirubinate with mucin. The formation of gallstones requires supersaturation of biliary cholesterol. Cholesterol is secreted into bile by hepatic cells with phospholipid, forming unilamellar vesicles. Bile salts dissolve the vesicles primarily in the gallbladder, forming mixed micelles. If the cholesterol-carrying capacity of the micelles and vesicles is exceeded, the bile becomes supersaturated, forming cholesterol monohydrate crystals. Nucleation is necessary for fusion of the supersaturated vesicles into large liquid crystals. Option B - Decreased concentration of bile calcium: Calcium bilirubinate is necessary for the formation of cholesterol stones. questions.solution: Correct Option B - Pancreatitis: Balloon dilation of the intact papilla has largely fallen out of favor due to the risk of pancreatitis. Bleeding is less common after dilation compared to sphincterotomy. Incorrect Options: Option A - Post-sphincterotomy bleeding: Post-sphincterotomy bleeding is more common after sphincterotomy, not after dilation of the intact biliary sphincter. Option C - Perforation: Perforation is uncommon with both procedures. questions.solution: Correct answer: B - Constipation can precede motor symptoms in some patients, but it is nonspecific and its prevalence and timing vary. questions.stem: A 61-year-old male with longstanding GERD and a history of Barrett’s esophagus undergoes surveillance endoscopy. No mucosal irregularities are seen, but four-quadrant biopsies are obtained of the 2.5 Barrett's segment. Dysplasia is noted on several of the histologic specimens. Which of the following is the next step in management?
questions.stemHtml: A 61-year-old male with longstanding GERD and a history of Barrett’s esophagus undergoes surveillance endoscopy. No mucosal irregularities are seen, but four-quadrant biopsies are obtained of the 2.5 Barrett's segment. Dysplasia is noted on several of the histologic specimens. Which of the following is the next step in management?

options.label: A
options.text: He should continue to undergo surveillance endoscopy to see if this develops into carcinoma.

options.label: B
options.text: He should undergo radiofrequency ablation therapy.

options.label: D
options.text: He should undergo endoscopic mucosal resection

questions.answerText: He should undergo endoscopic mucosal resection
questions.solution: Correct Option D - He should undergo endoscopic mucosal resection: The next step in management in a patient with Barrett's esophagus who is found to have dysplasia within a "short" (<3 cm) Barrett's segment or intramucosal carcinoma in a biopsy, is to perform staging studies (further biopsies, generally at every 1 cm), followed by endoscopic mucosal resection (EMR). Incorrect Options: Option A - He should continue to undergo surveillance endoscopy to see if this develops into carcinoma: This option is incorrect because dysplasia in Barrett's esophagus is considered a precancerous condition. When dysplasia is identified, it indicates an increased risk of developing esophageal carcinoma (cancer). As such, continued surveillance is not the appropriate course of action. Intervention is required to prevent the progression to carcinoma. Option B - He should undergo radiofrequency ablation therapy: This option is incorrect because radiofrequency ablation (RFA) therapy is typically used for the treatment of Barrett's esophagus with low-grade dysplasia or high-grade dysplasia that does not involve any visible cancer (carcinoma in situ). In this case, the patient has dysplasia on several histologic specimens, which may indicate a more advanced stage than what RFA can address. Endoscopic mucosal resection (EMR) or other treatments might be more suitable. Option C - He should undergo photodynamic therapy: This option is incorrect because photodynamic therapy (PDT) is used for treating high-grade dysplasia or early-stage esophageal carcinoma that is limited to the superficial layers of the esophagus (also known as intramucosal carcinoma). In this case, the patient has dysplasia but no visible mucosal irregularities, which suggests that PDT may not be the most appropriate treatment. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 65-year-old woman with a history of stroke complains of coughing and sputtering with wet swallows. What is the correct sequence of actions in the highly coordinated pharyngeal swallow response?
questions.stemHtml: A 65-year-old woman with a history of stroke complains of coughing and sputtering with wet swallows. What is the correct sequence of actions in the highly coordinated pharyngeal swallow response?

options.label: A
options.text: Nasopharyngeal closure by elevation and retraction of the soft palate → upper esophageal sphincter (UES) opening → laryngeal closure → tongue loading and pulsion→ pharyngeal clearance

options.label: B
options.text: Tongue loading and pulsion → nasopharyngeal closure by elevation and retraction of the soft palate → UES opening → laryngeal closure → pharyngeal clearance

options.label: C
options.text: Tongue loading and pulsion → laryngeal closure → nasopharyngeal closure by elevation and retraction of the soft palate → UES opening → pharyngeal clearance

options.label: D
options.text: Nasopharyngeal closure by elevation and retraction of the soft palate → tongue loading and pulsion → pharyngeal clearance → UES opening → laryngeal closure

questions.answerText: Nasopharyngeal closure by elevation and retraction of the soft palate → upper esophageal sphincter (UES) opening → laryngeal closure → tongue loading and pulsion→ pharyngeal clearance
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Nasopharyngeal closure by elevation and retraction of the soft palate → upper esophageal sphincter (UES) opening → laryngeal closure → tongue loading and pulsion→ pharyngeal clearance: The pharyngeal swallow rapidly configures pharyngeal structures from a respiratory to an alimentary pathway and then reverses this reconfiguration within 1 second. This is a highly coordinated response but can be dissected into separate actions. First there is nasopharyngeal closure by elevations and retraction of the soft palate. This is followed by upper esophageal sphincter opening and laryngeal closure. Tongue loading or ramping occurs followed by pulsion of the food bolus. This entire process is completed with clearance of the pharynx, stripping the last residue from the pharyngeal walls. Incorrect Options: Option B - Tongue loading and pulsion → nasopharyngeal closure by elevation and retraction of the soft palate → UES opening → laryngeal closure → pharyngeal clearance: The issue with option B is that it places "Tongue loading and pulsion" as the first step in the pharyngeal swallow response. However, the correct sequence starts with "Nasopharyngeal closure by elevation and retraction of the soft palate" as the initial action. Option C - Tongue loading and pulsion → laryngeal closure → nasopharyngeal closure by elevation and retraction of the soft palate → UES opening → pharyngeal clearance: The problem with option C is the order of actions. It places "Tongue loading and pulsion" before "laryngeal closure" and "nasopharyngeal closure by elevation and retraction of the soft palate." The correct sequence should start with "Nasopharyngeal closure" and end with "Pharyngeal clearance." Option D - Nasopharyngeal closure by elevation and retraction of the soft palate → tongue loading and pulsion → pharyngeal clearance → UES opening → laryngeal closure: The issue with option D is the order of actions as well. CT of the abdomen with contrast reveals an area of necrosis in the pancreatic head with gas in the tissue. Which of the following is true?

options.label: A
options.text: The finding of gas in the pancreatic bed is diagnostic of pancreatic infection.

options.label: B
options.text: Early open debridement and drainage of infected necrosis are associated with reduced mortality compared to minimally invasive drainage.

options.text: Needle aspiration with Gram stain and cultures does not reliably identify infection of the abscess.

questions.solution: Correct Option D - Minimally invasive debridement and/or drainage is indicated for infected necrosis: Even when treated prophylactically, patients with moderate to severe pancreatitis may develop infectious complications as a result of abscess formation or infected necrosis. Patients typically present a week or more after a hospital admission with increased pain, nausea or vomiting, fever, and/or leukocytosis, which are all associated with increased mortality. Any fluid collection or low-density area of the pancreas should undergo needle aspiration, and the aspirates should be Gram-stained and cultured, which has a 90% sensitivity and specificity for infection. questions.stem: You are evaluating a 48-year-old female patient with jaundice. She had cholecystectomy 3 months ago for symptomatic cholelithiasis. Her ALT and AST levels are 420 U/L and 380 U/L, and transabdominal ultrasound reveals dilation of intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts. Her serum CA 19-9 is 700. Which of the following is indicated next in the evaluation and management of this patient?
questions.stemHtml: You are evaluating a 48-year-old female patient with jaundice. She had cholecystectomy 3 months ago for symptomatic cholelithiasis. Her ALT and AST levels are 420 U/L and 380 U/L, and transabdominal ultrasound reveals dilation of intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts. Her serum CA 19-9 is 700. Which of the following is indicated next in the evaluation and management of this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option D - MRCP or EUS: This patient’s presentation is suggestive of an obstruction in the common bile duct, usually as the result of the passage of gallstones from the gallbladder. In patients who have undergone cholecystectomy, choledocholithiasis can occur from de novo stone formation or in the setting of escape of a gallstone during surgery. Confirmation of stones in the common bile duct is typically by MRCP or EUS. Patients at high risk of choledocholithiasis include those with acute cholangitis, presence of a CBD stone on transabdominal ultrasound, or elevated serum bilirubin greater than 4 mg/dL. In these groups, ERCP with stone removal is indicated. Although a dilated common bile duct seen on transabdominal ultrasound is suggestive of choledocholithiasis, it is important to realize that the common bile duct remains dilated to as much as 10 mm for up to 6 months after cholecystectomy. Incorrect Options: Option A - HIDA scan: HIDA scan would not provide clarification of the source of biliary obstruction. Option B - PET scan: PET scan is not indicated. The CA19-9 may be elevated in the absence of malignancy due to another cause of obstructive jaundice. Option C - Abdominal CT scan: Unenhanced CT is not a sensitive test. Although the addition of contrast increases sensitivity, it is not the diagnostic modality of choice for confirmation of CBD stone. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: While covering hospital GI consults, you are called to see a patient for evaluation of possible stress ulcer bleeding. Which of the following is true concerning stress ulcer bleeding?

options.label: A
options.text: Pharmacologic prophylaxis is effective for patients receiving enteral nutrition.

options.label: B
options.text: Stress ulceration usually occurs in the antrum or duodenum.

options.label: C
options.text: The primary mechanism of stress ulceration is excessive stimulation of parietal cells by gastrin stimulation.

options.text: Prolonged mechanical ventilation and coagulopathy are the most important risk factors for stress ulcer bleeding.

questions.answerText: Prolonged mechanical ventilation and coagulopathy are the most important risk factors for stress ulcer bleeding.
questions.solution: Option D - Prolonged mechanical ventilation and coagulopathy are the most important risk factors for stress ulcer bleeding: The most important risk factors for stress ulcer bleeding include coagulopathy (defined as a platelet count <50,000/m 3 ) and mechanical ventilation for longer than 48 hours. A history of GI ulcer or GI bleed within the past year, traumatic brain or spinal cord injury, and burn injury are high-risk characteristics that are indications for pharmacologic prophylaxis. Minor criteria include ICU stay >1 week, sepsis, occult GI bleed >6 days, and glucocorticoid therapy greater than the equivalent of 250 mg hydrocortisone. Incorrect Options: Option A - Pharmacologic prophylaxis is effective for patients receiving enteral nutrition: Enteral nutrition may reduce the risk of overt GI bleeding in patients with stress ulcers, but pharmacological prophylaxis may be harmful or ineffective in patients on enteral nutrition. Option B - Stress ulceration usually occurs in the antrum or duodenum: Stress ulcerations initially occur in the proximal portion of the stomach. After several days of hospitalization, stress ulcerations are generally more distal and deeper. Option C - The primary mechanism of stress ulceration is excessive stimulation of parietal cells by gastrin stimulation: Hypersecretion of acid due to excessive parietal cell stimulation by gastrin has been identified in head trauma patients, but this is most likely not the cause of stress ulceration in all ICU patients. Impaired mucosal protection results in critical patients as a result of destruction of the mucosal barrier by increased concentrations of bile salts or uremic toxins. Bicarbonate production that contributes to the mucosal defense barrier may also be diminished due to poor perfusion resulting from trauma, sepsis, or shock. @Neet_pg_bot

Vitals are as follows: BP 88/46 mmHg, HR 110 beats/minute, O2 saturation 92% on RA, respiratory rate 22 breaths/minute, and temperature 99.0 degrees Fahrenheit. CTA shows a large saddle PE. What is the most appropriate medication for acute treatment?
questions.stemHtml: A 67-year-old woman with breast cancer presents with chest pain and shortness of breath. The patient has a history of a hemorrhagic stroke 12 months ago. Vitals are as follows: BP 88/46 mmHg, HR 110 beats/minute, O2 saturation 92% on RA, respiratory rate 22 breaths/minute, and temperature 99.0 degrees Fahrenheit. CTA shows a large saddle PE. What is the most appropriate medication for acute treatment?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Heparin: This patient has a massive pulmonary embolism with hemodynamic instability. Although normally this is an indication for TPA, a history of hemorrhagic stroke is an absolute contraindication. Other absolute contraindications include recent ( <2 months) intracranial or spinal surgery or trauma, active bleeding or bleeding diathesis, or nonhemorrhagic stroke within the previous three months. Relative contraindications include severe uncontrolled hypertension, nonhemorrhagic stroke older than three months, surgery within the previous 10 days, and pregnancy. The patient should be started on heparin anticoagulation. Incorrect Options: Option A - TPA: In general, a patient with a PE and sustained hypotension would qualify for treatment with TPA. However, the history of a hemorrhagic CVA is an absolute contraindication. Option C - Warfarin: While this patient may eventually be bridged to warfarin for long-term anticoagulation, this is not an acute treatment for PE. Option D - IVC filter: IVC filters are generally indicated if anticoagulation is contraindicated. An IVC filter is not an acute treatment. Anticoagulation with heparin should be started first. @Neet_pg_bot

He reports attending a picnic 3 days ago in warm weather and eating homemade potato salad that had been unrefrigerated for several hours. On physical examination, he is afebrile with a heart rate of 120 beats/minute and a blood pressure of 95/65 mmHg. A basic laboratory evaluation reveals an elevated hemoglobin level of 18 g/dL and a hematocrit of 54%. What is the most likely cause of this patient’s polycythemia?

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Volume depletion: In this patient with 2 days of fluid loss due to possible food poisoning, volume depletion is almost certain Polycythemia is defined as an abnormally elevated hemoglobin or hematocrit. It can be classified as relative polycythemia (spuriously elevated due to volume depletion) or absolute polycythemia (accompanied by an increased red blood cell mass). Patients with relative polycythemia often have a clinical history and physical examination consistent with volume depletion as well as a normal red blood cell mass. Treatment involves volume repletion and addressing the underlying cause. Absolute polycythemia may be caused by an increased production of red blood cells (primary polycythemia) or by a response to increased erythropoietin leading to an increased red blood cell mass (secondary polycythemia). In this patient with 2 days of fluid loss due to possible food poisoning, volume depletion is almost certain. Incorrect Options: Option A - JAK-2 mutation: JAK-2 mutation causes polycythemia vera. Option C - Pheochromocytoma: Pheochromocytoma can cause paraneoplastic syndrome leading to increased erythropoietin levels, which can result in polycythemia. Option D - Erythropoietin injections: Erythropoietin injections may be abused by athletes to increase oxygen utilization and improve endurance. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman presents to her physician with new onset fatigue and malaise. She quantifies her fatigue as able to climb just 1 flight of stairs as against 4 flights of stairs as before. She doesn’t give any history of loss of appetite, weight loss or any bleeding manifestations. Screening labs reveal the following: Hb 7.8mg/dl Hct 22.6 RBC 4.8 × 1012/ L Plt 14,000 WBC 300/ microL MCV 90 fL absolute neutrophil count 0.1 absolute lymphocyte count 0.1 absolute eosinophil count 0.1 LFT and RFT Normal The patient is referred to a haematologist and undergoes a bone marrow biopsy. The bone marrow examination fails to detect an increase in the percentage of blasts and also does not show marked dysplasia in any of the three cells lines. No malignant clone is detected by flow cytometry. Megakaryocytes appear normal. The overall cellularity of the marrow is noted to be 5% and much of the marrow space is occupied by fat cells. The patient has a sibling who with 10/10 histocompatibility. Which of the following is the most appropriate consideration for first-line therapy for this patient?

The patient is referred to a haematologist and undergoes a bone marrow biopsy. The bone marrow examination fails to detect an increase in the percentage of blasts and also does not show marked dysplasia in any of the three cells lines. No malignant clone is detected by flow cytometry. Megakaryocytes appear normal. The overall cellularity of the marrow is noted to be 5% and much of the marrow space is occupied by fat cells.
The patient has a sibling who with 10/10 histocompatibility.
Which of the following is the most appropriate consideration for first-line therapy for this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Allogeneic stem cell transplant: Aplastic anaemia is a clinical syndrome caused by decreased bone marrow haematopoiesis resulting in pancytopenia. Diagnosis of aplastic anaemia requires presence of anaemia (Hb <10 gm/dL), neutropenia (neutrophil count of <1500/uL), thrombocytopenia (platelet count <50,000/uL) and absolute reticulocytopenia (reticulocyte <40,000/uL) accompanied by a hypocellular marrow without fibrosis or malignant cells. Cytotoxic T-cell-mediated destruction of hematopoietic stem cells plays an important role in the pathogenesis of aplastic anaemia. In the presence of HLA matched sibling donor, allogeneic stem cell transplantation should be first line therapy in patients under the age of 40 years. Combined immunosuppressive therapy with ATG and cyclosporine should be the first line therapy in all patients without a matched sibling donor as well as in patients over 40 years of age with a matched sibling. Incorrect Options: Option A - High-dose combination cytotoxic chemotherapy : This option is primarily used for malignant hematological diseases, such as acute leukemias. Given that the bone marrow biopsy did not reveal any malignant cells or increased blasts, this patient's presentation is not consistent with a malignant process. Therefore, this aggressive approach would not be appropriate. Option B - Immune therapy (eg CsA) + Eltrombopag : This is a primary treatment approach for patients with SAA who don't have a suitable donor for transplantation. Immunosuppressive therapy, especially the combination of antithymocyte globulin (ATG) and cyclosporine (CsA), has been shown to improve blood counts in a significant proportion of patients. Eltrombopag is an oral thrombopoietin receptor agonist that can also be added to improve response. This treatment would be appropriate for patients without a matched sibling donor or for those who are older than 40. However, in the given scenario, the patient has an available sibling donor, making stem cell transplant a more suitable choice. Option D - Supportive care and watchful waiting : This approach is typically used for older patients with non-severe aplastic anemia or those who don't have any other available treatment options. Given the severity of the patient's pancytopenia and her age, merely providing supportive care without definitive therapy would place her at risk for life-threatening complications like infections due to neutropenia. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: You see an infant with Diamond-Blackfan anemia. The patient’s family states that had a consultation with pediatric cardiology. Which of the listed congenital heart disease anomalies is most common in Diamond-Blackfan anemia?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Ventricular septal defect: Diamond-Blackfan anemia (DBA) is primarily characterized by red cell aplasia, but many patients also present with congenital abnormalities. Among these, cardiac defects are notably significant. In DBA, ventricular septal defect is the most commonly reported cardiovascular pathology. In one specific review, a VSD was documented in 44% of DBA patients, making it the most frequent congenital heart disease anomaly associated with the condition. Incorrect Options: Option B - Mitral valve prolapse: While mitral valve prolapse can be seen in various conditions and might be present in some DBA patients, it is not the most commonly reported cardiac defect in DBA as compared to VSD. Option C - Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: Similarly, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, which is an increase in the thickness of the myocardium, isn't the most common cardiac anomaly in DBA patients. Instead, structural defects like VSD have a higher incidence. Option D - Coarctation of the aorta: This refers to a narrowing of the aorta. The mentioned review indicates that coarctation of the aorta was seen in 4.4% of DBA patients. Though it's a significant finding, it's less common than VSD in the context of DBA @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 32 year old female G3P3 with a h/o multiple uterine fibroids induced DUB after uterine artery embolization is transfused with RBCs. During the transfusion she develops nausea, chills, rigors, and mild dyspnea. Her temperature is 38.4 ° C. Work-up for hemolysis is negative. How should this patient be managed?
questions.stemHtml: A 32 year old female G3P3 with a h/o multiple uterine fibroids induced DUB after uterine artery embolization is transfused with RBCs. During the transfusion she develops nausea, chills, rigors, and mild dyspnea. Her temperature is 38.4 ° C. Work-up for hemolysis is negative. How should this patient be managed?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Acetaminophen: This patient's presentation is most consistent with a febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reaction (FNHTR). Appropriately named, patients present with a fever (a temperature rise > 1°C) without hemolysis after a transfusion. FNHTR is common and can occur during or ~1 to 6 hours after a transfusion of red cells or platelets. Additional symptoms can include headache, nausea, vomiting, chills, rigors, mild dyspnea, and hypotension. Patients are managed with reassurance, acetaminophen (an antipyretic), and occasionally meperidine (for rigors). Incorrect Options: Option A - Lasix: Lasix (furosemide) is a loop diuretic commonly used to treat fluid retention. It would not be the appropriate choice for managing febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reactions (FNHTR), which are characterized by fever, chills, and rigors, rather than fluid overload. Option C - Epinephrine, Benadryl, and Corticosteroids: This combination of medications is used to manage severe allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis, during transfusion. Anaphylaxis presents with more severe symptoms such as difficulty breathing, hypotension, and potentially life-threatening symptoms. The patient's symptoms in this scenario (fever, chills, rigors, mild dyspnea) are more consistent with FNHTR, not anaphylaxis. Option D - Supportive Care and Ventilatory Support: Supportive care and ventilatory support are indeed the management options for transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI), which presents with acute respiratory distress, bilateral pulmonary infiltrates, and hypoxemia. However, these symptoms are not present in the given patient's case. The patient's symptoms of fever, chills, rigors, and mild dyspnea are more indicative of FNHTR. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: What is the purpose of radiating packed red blood cells?
questions.stemHtml: What is the purpose of radiating packed red blood cells?

options.label: B
options.text: Diminish transfusion related graft versus host disease

options.label: C
options.text: Diminish the incidence of cmv transmission

options.label: D
options.text: Diminish the incidence of all viral infections

questions.answerText: Diminish transfusion related graft versus host disease
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Diminish Transfusion-Related Graft Versus Host Disease (GVHD): Graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) is a potentially life-threatening complication that occurs when immune cells from a donor (graft) attack the recipient's (host's) tissues. GVHD is a significant concern, especially in individuals with compromised immune systems, such as patients who have undergone allogeneic stem cell transplantation. When blood products containing viable T-lymphocytes are transfused into these patients, these immune cells can recognize the host's tissues as foreign and mount an immune response, leading to GVHD. By irradiating packed red blood cells, the T-lymphocytes present in the blood product are effectively deactivated, preventing them from proliferating and causing an immune response in the recipient. This minimizes the risk of developing transfusion-related GVHD, which can have serious clinical consequences. Incorrect Options: Option A - Diminish Febrile Transfusion Reaction: Febrile transfusion reactions are characterized by fever and chills in response to a blood transfusion. Irradiation of packed red blood cells is not primarily used to address febrile transfusion reactions; these reactions are often related to other factors, such as antibodies or cytokines in the blood product. Option C - Diminish the Incidence of CMV Transmission: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) transmission can occur through blood transfusion. While irradiation can reduce the risk of CMV transmission, its primary purpose is to prevent GVHD rather than CMV transmission. Option D - Diminish the Incidence of All Viral Infections: Irradiation primarily targets T-lymphocytes to prevent GVHD, and it is not a comprehensive method for reducing the risk of all viral infections. Other measures, such as proper screening and testing of blood products, are employed to address viral infections in transfusion recipients. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option A - Clearance a factor X by amyloid protein in the liver: In light chain (AL) amyloidosis, which is characterized by the deposition of abnormal amyloid protein fibrils in various organs, including the kidneys and heart, clotting factor abnormalities can occur due to the interaction of amyloid proteins with clotting factors. Amyloid fibrils can adsorb clotting factors, particularly factor X, leading to increased clearance of these factors from the circulation. This reduced availability of factor X impairs the normal clotting cascade, resulting in prolonged PT (prothrombin time) and aPTT (activated partial thromboplastin time). This mechanism contributes to the bleeding tendency seen in some patients with amyloidosis. questions.solution: Correct Option C- 3 g/m²: High-dose cytarabine (2-3g/m²) is typically utilized for consolidation in younger, fit patients following successful induction. Incorrect Options: Option A- 100 mg/m²: This is considered a low dose of cytarabine. While intermediate doses might be utilized in certain contexts, for consolidation therapy in younger fit patients with good-risk AML, the high dose (2-3g/m²) has been demonstrated to be superior. Flow cytometry reveals that he has acute myeloid leukemia. Bone marrow biopsy confirmed that he now has transformation to AML, with 35% blasts. Molecular studies show that he has detectable BCR-ABL p210 transcripts. Cytogenetics are sent. Mutation analysis does not reveal a new activating mutation. What is the ideal mode of management?

options.label: C

questions.solution: Correct Option D- Daunorubicin plus cytarabine plus imatinib: The patient's presentation and clinical course suggest that he has transformed from chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) to acute myeloid leukemia (AML) in blast crisis. Blast crisis is an aggressive transformation of CML where the disease shifts from a chronic phase to an acute leukemia-like phase. In this phase, there is a rapid increase in the number of immature myeloid cells (blasts) in the bone marrow and peripheral blood. The management approach for a patient with CML in blast crisis involves combining treatment strategies for both AML and CML. This means using intensive chemotherapy to induce remission in the AML component, while also targeting the underlying CML with tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) to reduce the BCR-ABL activity. Daunorubicin plus cytarabine plus imatinib, reflects this combined approach. Daunorubicin and cytarabine are standard chemotherapy agents used in the induction regimen for AML.Imatinib, which is a first-generation TKI targeting BCR-ABL, is included to continue controlling the underlying CML component. This combined treatment aims to achieve remission . Incorrect Options: Option A- "HyperCVAD + imatinib": HyperCVAD is a chemotherapy regimen commonly used in the treatment of acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) but is not typically employed as a first-line treatment for AML. Moreover, since the patient already has CML with evidence of blast crisis, using only HyperCVAD would not adequately address the underlying CML component, and imatinib alone might not be sufficient to manage the disease. Option B- "Daunorubicin plus cytarabine": This choice involves the standard induction chemotherapy for AML, but it lacks the targeting of the BCR-ABL abnormality seen in CML. Given the patient's history of CML, it's important to continue TKI therapy like imatinib to address both aspects of the disease. Option C- "Change to second generation tyrosine kinase inhibitor, provide supportive care and wait to assess response": While switching to a second-generation TKI might be considered in CML management, this choice does not address the acute myeloid transformation (AML) which is the primary concern at this point. Waiting to assess response without initiating appropriate treatment for AML can lead to disease progression and worsen the patient's condition. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option D - Takayasu's arteritis: Presentation of Takayasu's arteritis is often with constitutional symptoms such as fever, weight loss, night sweats and arthralgias. Symptoms related to ischaemia may include ischaemic stroke and/or transient ischaemic attacks, visual disturbances and rarely in children-claudication. The aortic arch is commonly involved, but the thoracoabdominal aorta and its branches, as well as the pulmonary artery, can be affected. If the aortic arch is involved there may be differential BP and absent or diminished upper arm pulses with bruits over the diseased vessels. Post-stenotic dilatations may result in bounding pulses. Hypertension is a common complication and may be due to renal artery stenosis. Major complications include cardiac failure, aortic regurgitation, or coronary artery involvement. CT angiograms, MRA and FDG-PET scanning are all useful in diagnosis (see Update of the EULAR recommendations 2018). Rarely inflammatory markers are normal so a high index of clinical suspicion is required. The mainstay of treatment is immunosuppression with steroids and methotrexate. Additionally, the laboratory findings and weight loss are not typical of cervical rib, making it a less likely diagnosis. questions.solution: Correct Option C: Echocardiography Antiphospholipid syndrome was first described by Hughes in 1983. The most common cardiac manifestation of the disease is non-bacterial thrombotic endocarditis, caused by platelet-fibrin thrombi forming on the endocardial surface of valves, with a prevalence of 11.6% reported. An echocardiogram is an essential investigation for any patient presenting with a cerebral embolism to exclude an underlying cardiac cause such as mural thrombus, atrial myxoma, valvular vegetations, patent foramen ovale, an atrial or ventricular septal defects. Since her lupus anticoagulant and anticardiolipin antibodies are both positive, testing for anti-beta2 glycoprotein1 antibodies would not provide any additional information at this stage. A repeat antiphospholipid screen in 12 weeks' time may be considered, but this is not relevant to this particular question. At her age, she is unlikely to have significant atherosclerotic involvement of her carotid arteries to warrant a carotid arterial Doppler. If a paradoxical embolus was suspected, then an echocardiogram would be more urgently required than a venous Doppler scan of the leg. Her history does not suggest cerebral vasculitis or encephalitis and therefore MRI would not take precedence over echocardiography in this case. questions.solution: Correct Options A - Aortic dissection: Patients with GCA can develop disease in non-cranial vascular territories. Studies suggest between 3-18% of patients with GCA will suffer from aortitis, and it is the leading cause of inflammatory aortitis. The risk appears to increase with the severity of inflammation and other traditional cardiovascular risks. The ascending aorta is most often affected. However recognising it is difficult as it is often asymptomatic. It should be considered in all patients with GCA with very active inflammatory symptoms (fever, weight loss etc) and high inflammatory markers. Once dissection occurs it commonly presents with acute central chest pain often radiating through to the back. There may be a difference in blood pressure between the arms, a difference of >20 mmHg should be of concern. Depending on where the dissection is there may be neurological symptoms and signs. Induction therapy with either intravenous cyclophosphamide or oral mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) is discussed with her to treat lupus nephritis. After going through the risks and benefits of each treatment, she opts for MMF. What is the target dose of MMF to treat her lupus nephritis?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - 3 grams daily: This patient has marked lupus nephritis which requires aggressive treatment to prevent deterioration towards end-stage renal disease necessitating renal replacement therapy. Currently, for lupus nephritis class III or IV, the BSR recommends either intravenous cyclophosphamide via Euro-Lupus regimen of 500 mg fortnightly (total 3 grams) or oral MMF with a target dose of 3 grams daily (1.5 g BD) for 6 months. Head-to-head trial data show that MMF is non-inferior to cyclophosphamide. For class V, the BSR recommends MMF over cyclophosphamide due to superior efficacy/toxicity ratio. If this patient was to relapse or developed significant adverse features with MMF, she should then be offered cyclophosphamide. Beyond this, other treatments such as calcineurin inhibitors and rituximab should be considered. Incorrect Options: Option A - 0.5 grams daily: 0.5 grams daily is not recommended to treat the patient condition Option C - 1.5 grams daily: This dose is not recommended to treat the patient condition Option D - 2 grams daily: MMF can also be used as maintenance therapy with a target dose of 2 grams daily (1 g BD). @Neet_pg_bot

As a result, the affected individuals develop Na loss (salt wasting), hypovolaemia, hypocalciuria, hypomagnesaemia and metabolic alkalosis. questions.stem: A 70-year-old man has a history of hypertension, which is adequately controlled with doxazosin yet has persistent hypokalaemia. The patient is referred to the clinic as the potassium is persistently between 2.6-3.1 mEq/L. Investigations show a plasma renin activity: aldosterone ratio of 780. What is the most appropriate management option for this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 70-year-old man has a history of hypertension, which is adequately controlled with doxazosin yet has persistent hypokalaemia. The patient is referred to the clinic as the potassium is persistently between 2.6-3.1 mEq/L. Investigations show a plasma renin activity: aldosterone ratio of 780. What is the most appropriate management option for this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: Switch Doxazosin to an ACE inhibitor

options.label: D
options.text: Switch Doxazosin to a Thiazide diuretic

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Start a Potassium supplement: The initial screening test for the diagnosis of primary aldosteronism is a measurement of a plasma renin activity to aldosterone ratio. A ratio above 1000 is highly suggestive of primary hyperaldosteronism. (In the UK this is used and in the US they often quote the other way around i.e. aldo:renin ratio (ARR) where a ratio of >20 is suggestive of a diagnosis of primary aldosteronism). However false positives and negatives can occur. Some medications can interfere with aldosterone/ renin levels. Also if the patient is hypokalaemic, aldosterone concentrations can fall and marginal increases in renin can make for a false negative result. Oral potassium supplements are given to avoid any false-negative test results. A false-negative result can also be obtained in patients with chronic renal failure due to persistently elevated renin levels. Incorrect Options: Option A - Switch Doxazosin to an ACE inhibitor : ACE Inhibitor would not be the best approach because ACE inhibitors may exacerbate hyperkalemia (high potassium levels), which is a concern in this patient. Option C - Switch Doxazosin to spironolactone : Spironolactone is a potassium-sparing diuretic and would be a suitable long-term treatment option to counteract the effects of excess aldosterone and potassium loss. However, considering the patient's persistently low potassium levels, it is important to promptly address the hypokalemia with a potassium supplement ( option b ), while evaluating and planning further management. Option D - Switch Doxazosin to a Thiazide diuretic : Thiazide diuretic would likely worsen the hypokalemia by further increasing potassium loss. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option A - Secondary adrenal insufficiency: In an SST, blood for baseline plasma cortisol and ACTH are first collected. Serum cortisol should rise to a peak of 550 nmol/L. As there are significant variations among different cortisol assays, the cut-off for a normal cortisol response must be laboratory-specific or assay-specific (ranging from 420 to 574 nmol/L). On examination, her BMI is 30 kg/m2 and her blood pressure is 144/86 mmHg. Investigations reveal a fasting plasma glucose of 5.6 % and an HbA1c of 9% ( below 6 is the normal). Which of the following would favour a diagnosis of type 2 rather than type 1 diabetes for this lady?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Presence of background retinopathy: HDL-C concentrations are higher in patients with type 1 diabetes, while up to 20% of patients with type 2 diabetes will demonstrate evidence of microvascular complications at diagnosis which will not be the case in patients with type 1 diabetes. Incorrect Options: Option A - Autoimmune aetiology of hypothyroidism: Autoimmune etiology of hypothyroidism The presence of an autoimmune etiology of hypothyroidism (Hashimoto's thyroiditis) is not specific to either type 1 or type 2 diabetes. It is more commonly associated with type 1 diabetes, but it can also be seen in type 2 diabetes. Option C - High HDL cholesterol level: High HDL cholesterol level The level of HDL cholesterol is not specific to the type of diabetes and can vary widely among individuals with both type 1 and type 2 diabetes. Option D - Normal albumin/creatinine ratio: Normal albumin/creatinine ratio The albumin/creatinine ratio is a marker of kidney function and is used to assess the risk of diabetic nephropathy. A normal albumin/creatinine ratio does not provide significant information to differentiate between type 1 and type 2 diabetes. @Neet_pg_bot
