questions.solution: Correct Option D - Pioglitazone: This gentleman has non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) as evidenced by deranged liver function tests and fatty infiltration on ultrasound scan. NASH is commonly seen in type 2 diabetes and is associated with an increased body mass index. It usually resembles alcoholic liver disease but the history of alcohol intake in such people is either absent or only modest. The diagnosis of this condition is based on the exclusion of common liver disorders like viral hepatitis, alcoholic liver disease, drug-induced and autoimmune liver disease (e.g. primary biliary cirrhosis). The gold standard confirmatory test for diagnosis is liver biopsy although this is rarely done as can be supported with non-invasive tests. Incorrect Options: Option A - Liraglutide: It is a glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1 RA), which is also used to treat type 2 diabetes. It has shown benefits in reducing HbA1c and weight loss. However, in a patient with deranged liver function tests, pioglitazone may be a more appropriate choice. Option B - Insulin: It may be considered in patients with uncontrolled diabetes when other oral medications fail to achieve glycemic targets. However, in this case, pioglitazone can be considered before starting insulin therapy. Option C - Empagliflozin: It is a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitor, which is also used to treat type 2 diabetes. While it has shown cardiovascular and renal benefits in certain populations, it may not be the best choice in this patient with deranged liver function tests. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 34-year-old female came to the clinic with complaints of nausea, vomiting, and sudden onset severe right-sided flank pain radiating to the groin for the last 7 days. The pain is not associated with fever and chills, but she has reported urinary frequency and urgency. She is a smoker and has not been sexually active. Urine pregnancy test is negative. She has had ulcerative colitis for the last 6 years and is taking sulfasalazine and steroids. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the pain?
questions.stemHtml: A 34-year-old female came to the clinic with complaints of nausea, vomiting, and sudden onset severe right-sided flank pain radiating to the groin for the last 7 days. The pain is not associated with fever and chills, but she has reported urinary frequency and urgency. She is a smoker and has not been sexually active. Urine pregnancy test is negative. She has had ulcerative colitis for the last 6 years and is taking sulfasalazine and steroids. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the pain?
questions.solution: Correct Option C: Calcium oxalate stones This patient has developed sudden onset severe unilateral flank pain, nausea, and vomiting with underlying inflammatory bowel disease, most likely suggesting that she has calcium oxalate stones. Calcium oxalate is the most common stone. The underlying etiologies include hypercalciuria, hyperoxaluria, vitamin C abuse, and ethylene glycol poisoning. In ulcerative colitis, there is fat malabsorption leading to increased fatty acids. Calcium binds these fatty acids, resulting in increased levels of free oxalate, increasing oxalate absorption from the intestine. Most calculi originate within the kidney and proceed distally, creating various degrees of urinary obstruction as they become lodged in narrow areas. The location and quality of pain are related to the position of the stone within the urinary tract. The severity of pain is related to the degree of obstruction, presence of ureteral spasm, and presence of any associated infection. Urine microscopy will reveal octahedron-shaped crystals. These stones are radio-opaque in nature, so these stones are visible on an X-ray or CT scan. Incorrect options: Option A: Ectopic pregnancy Patients with ectopic pregnancy can present with nausea, vomiting, and unilateral flank pain. In ectopic pregnancy, the patient may present with hemodynamic instability. This is less likely in this patient as she is not sexually active. Option B: Ovarian torsion Ovarian torsion can present with sudden abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. It usually occurs after physical activity and is common in patients with ovarian cysts or masses. The pain of ovarian torsion is dull and continuous and it does not radiate to the groin. Option D: Struvite stones These stones occur after urinary tract infection by urease-positive organisms, i.e. Proteus mirabilis and Klebsiella. These stones are large and block the renal papillae. These are not formed in patients with ulcerative colitis. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with a history of bladder cancer complains of dull, throbbing flank pain and hematuria. His history is positive for recurrent urinary tract infections. On imaging, a massive staghorn calculus of around 5 cm is seen in his left kidney, as shown below. What is the best management strategy for this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 60-year-old man with a history of bladder cancer complains of dull, throbbing flank pain and hematuria. His history is positive for recurrent urinary tract infections. On imaging, a massive staghorn calculus of around 5 cm is seen in his left kidney, as shown below. What is the best management strategy for this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option B: Percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL) Staghorn calculi are massive, branching stones that occupy a major amount of the renal pelvis and, if left untreated, can cause significant blockage and kidney damage. Percutaneous nephrolithotomy is the most effective method for treating these stones and decreasing the risk of consequences. Antibiotics may also be required to treat any related infection. Percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL) is a minimally invasive surgical treatment for large or complicated kidney stones, such as struvite stones. A small incision in the patient's back is made, and specialized tools are used to access and remove the stone from the kidney. PCNL is often prescribed for individuals with large or complex struvite stones that cannot adequately treat with conventional procedures such as shock wave lithotripsy or ureteroscopy. PCNL has various advantages for the treatment of struvite stones aside from its effectiveness: PCNL enables the thorough removal of the stone, lowering the risk of recurring infections or stone development. Lower complication risk: Because PCNL is a minimally invasive treatment, it has a lower complication rate than traditional open surgery. Individuals who undergo PCNL often have shorter hospital stays and faster recovery times than those who undergo open surgery. Incorrect options: Option A: Oral tamsulosin When a kidney stone goes through the ureter, it can create spasms in the ureter's muscles, resulting in pain and difficulty passing the stone. Tamsulosin is an alpha-blocker and is thought to operate by relaxing these muscles, which can aid in the passage of the stone. It is useful in the case of very small stones if the size of the stone is less than 5mm Option C: Extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy (ESWL) Extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy (ESWL) is a non-invasive therapy used to treat kidney stones, especially struvite stones. ESWL uses shock waves to break up the stone into tiny fragments that can be passed out of the body through urine. ESWL is usually recommended for struvite stones less than 2 cm in diameter and situated in the kidney or upper ureter. The method is less effective for larger stones or stones positioned in the lower ureter because the shock waves may not be able to reach the stone efficiently. Option D: Oral allopurinol Allopurinol is a medicine often used to treat gout and prevent the production of kidney uric acid stones. Allopurinol works by lowering uric acid production in the body, which prevents uric acid buildup in the blood and urine, which can lead to gout attacks or kidney stone formation. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 10-year-old male patient presents to the clinic with a history of recurrent urinary tract infections and abdominal pain. His family history reveals that his older brother died from an end-stage renal disease at 12yrs. On physical examination, the abdomen is distended, and palpation reveals bilateral flank masses. Which diagnostic test is the most appropriate initial step in the evaluation of this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 10-year-old male patient presents to the clinic with a history of recurrent urinary tract infections and abdominal pain. His family history reveals that his older brother died from an end-stage renal disease at 12yrs. On physical examination, the abdomen is distended, and palpation reveals bilateral flank masses. Which diagnostic test is the most appropriate initial step in the evaluation of this patient?

options.label: B
options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the abdomen

questions.solution: Correct Option C: Ultrasound of the abdomen Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease (ARPKD) is a rare genetic disorder that affects the kidneys and other organs. It is characterised by the formation of cysts in the kidneys that can lead to renal failure. ARPKD is caused by mutations in the PKHD1 gene, chromosome locus 6p12.2 and is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern. The disease typically presents in infancy or childhood and can be associated with abnormalities such as hepatic fibrosis, portal hypertension, and congenital heart disease. The diagnostic test of choice for ARPKD is an ultrasound of the abdomen. This non-invasive, cost-effective, and safe imaging modality can detect the presence of renal cysts and hepatic fibrosis. This image shows ARPK with a normal kidney below Ultrasound is also useful in monitoring disease progression and response to treatment. Incorrect options: Option A: Renal biopsy Renal biopsy is an invasive procedure not routinely used to diagnose ARPKD. It may be used in certain cases to confirm the diagnosis or evaluate for complications such as nephrotic syndrome, but it is not the initial step in the evaluation of this patient. Option B: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the abdomen MRI of the abdomen is a useful imaging modality in the evaluation of renal cysts and hepatic fibrosis in patients with ARPKD. However, it is more expensive and less readily available than ultrasound. MRI may be used if the ultrasound is inconclusive or further evaluation is required. Option D: Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen CT of the abdomen is not the preferred imaging modality in the evaluation of ARPKD. CT exposes the patient to ionising radiation, which can increase the risk of cancer, and it is more expensive than ultrasound. CT may be used if the ultrasound is inconclusive or further evaluation is required. @Neet_pg_bot

Vesicoureteral reflux

  • Vesicoureteral reflux (VUR) is the retrograde flow of urine from the bladder into the ureter and kidneys 
  • Pathogenesis 
    • Chronic retrograde flow of urine due to VUR increases the pressure within the lumen of the nephron as well as a dilated calyceal system causes compression of surrounding blood vessels
    • Decreased blood flow through these vessels leads to decreased perfusion of kidneys, followed by ischemia that leads to tubular atrophy and thinning of the renal cortex and medulla

  • The proliferation of the mesangium and matrix expansion occur secondary to the deposition of IgA-based immune complex in the mesangium, which is classically seen in IgA nephropathy
  • IgA nephropathy causes a nephritic syndrome that presents with hematuria, hypertension, and mild proteinuria 
  • IgA nephropathy develops during an infection, i.e. respiratory and gastrointestinal, known as synpharyngitic

  • Thickening of the glomerular basement membrane giving rise to prominent glomerular capillary loops is a classical feature of membranous nephropathy 
  • Membranous nephropathy gives rise to the nephrotic syndrome that manifests as proteinuria, body swelling, hypercoagulable state, hyperlipidemia, and increased risk of infection

What is the most appropriate management option for this patient?

options.label: C
options.text: Refer for transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP)

questions.solution: Correct Option A: Starting alpha-blocker therapy It is the first-line treatment for patients with mild to moderate symptoms of BPH. Alpha-blockers such as tamsulosin and alfuzosin relax the smooth muscle of the prostate and bladder neck, improving urine flow and reducing symptoms. They are generally well-tolerated and have minimal side effects. Side effects- Dizziness, headache, upper respiratory infection symptoms First-dose hypotension, fatigue, and edema may exacerbate symptoms of congestive heart failure Incorrect options: Option B: Starting 5-alpha reductase inhibitor therapy It is recommended for patients with moderate to severe symptoms of BPH and a large prostate volume. 5-alpha reductase inhibitors such as finasteride and dutasteride inhibit the conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone, which is the hormone that promotes prostate growth. They can reduce the size of the prostate and improve urinary symptoms, but they may take several months to show effect. Side effects-Decreased libido, gynecomastia, ejaculatory disorders, impotence Option C: Referring for transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP) It is recommended for patients with severe symptoms of BPH that are refractory to medical therapy or for patients with complications such as recurrent urinary tract infections, bladder stones, or urinary retention. TURP is a surgical procedure that involves the removal of the prostate tissue that is obstructing urine flow. Indications for TURP Acute Retention of Urine Significant symptoms from BOO not responsive to tablets Persistent or recurrent UTI Significant bleeding (if due to Prostate) Bladder stones secondary to bladder outlet obstruction Option D: Performing prostate-specific antigen (PSA) test It is unnecessary as the patient's symptoms and physical examination suggest BPH. questions.stem: A 45-year-old male presents with flank pain and hematuria. Imaging studies revealed a 5-cm mass in the upper pole of his right kidney with areas of necrosis and calcification. Immunohistochemical staining shows positive staining for CD10 and negative staining for cytokeratin 7. What is the most likely subtype of renal cell carcinoma?
questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old male presents with flank pain and hematuria. Imaging studies revealed a 5-cm mass in the upper pole of his right kidney with areas of necrosis and calcification. Immunohistochemical staining shows positive staining for CD10 and negative staining for cytokeratin 7. What is the most likely subtype of renal cell carcinoma?
questions.solution: Correct Option A: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma Based on the clinical presentation, imaging studies, and immunohistochemical staining pattern, the most likely subtype of renal cell carcinoma is clear cell renal cell carcinoma (RCC). This subtype of renal cell carcinoma is the most common, accounting for approximately 75% of all cases. It typically presents with necrosis and calcifications on imaging studies and is characterized by the presence of clear cytoplasm due to the accumulation of lipids and glycogen. Positive staining for CD10 is a characteristic feature of clear cell renal cell carcinoma, while negative staining for cytokeratin 7 can help differentiate it from other subtypes of renal cell carcinoma, such as papillary and chromophobe. Clear cell RCC is associated with mutations in the von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) gene, which regulates hypoxia-inducible factors (HIFs) and the oxygen-sensing pathway. Incorrect options: Option B: Papillary renal cell carcinoma Papillary RCC is the second most common type of renal cell carcinoma, accounting for approximately 10-15% of all cases. It typically presents as a mass in the kidney and can be associated with hematuria and flank pain. In imaging studies, it is characterized by cystic areas within the tumor. The tumor cells have a papillary growth pattern and can be classified into two subtypes: type 1 and type 2. Type 1 tumors have a better prognosis than type 2 tumors. Papillary renal cell carcinoma is associated with mutations in the MET proto-oncogene, which is involved in cell proliferation and survival. Option C: Chromophobe renal cell carcinoma Chromophobe RCC is a rare subtype of renal cell carcinoma, accounting for approximately 5% of all cases. It typically presents as a mass in the kidney and can be associated with hematuria and flank pain. On imaging studies, it is characterized by a well-circumscribed mass with a homogeneous appearance. The tumor cells have pale, eosinophilic cytoplasm and a perinuclear halo. Chromophobe renal cell carcinoma is associated with mutations in the gene encoding for the mitochondrial protein, succinate dehydrogenase (SDHB). Option D: Collecting duct carcinoma Collecting duct carcinoma is a rare subtype of renal cell carcinoma, accounting for less than 1% of all cases. It typically presents as a mass in the kidney and can be associated with hematuria, flank pain, and fever. On imaging studies, it is characterized by a poorly defined mass with irregular borders. The tumors have a glandular or tubular growth pattern and can resemble transitional cell carcinoma of the bladder. Collecting duct carcinoma is associated with mutations in genes involved in the maintenance of the collecting ducts of the kidney. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: A 4-year-old girl is brought to her paediatrician with abdominal pain and a palpable mass in her abdomen. She has also been experiencing nausea and vomiting for the past few days. On physical examination, the paediatrician feels a large mass on the right side of the abdomen that extends to the midline. An abdominal ultrasound confirms the presence of a mass arising from the right kidney. The paediatrician suspects Wilms's tumor and refers the child to an oncologist for further evaluation. Which of the following is a characteristic histological finding of Wilms tumor?
questions.solution: Correct Option D. Blastemal proliferation Wilms tumor, also known as nephroblastoma, is a malignant kidney tumour that arises from immature renal cells. It is the most common type of kidney cancer in children, accounting for approximately 6% of all childhood cancers. Wilms tumour is most commonly diagnosed in children under the age of 5, with a peak incidence between 3 and 4 years of age. The clinical presentation of Wilms tumour varies depending on the size and location of the tumour. The most common presenting symptom is a painless, palpable abdominal mass found in up to 90% of cases. Abdominal pain is also a common symptom and is reported in approximately 25-30% of cases. Hematuria, anaemia, fever, and weight loss can also be associated with Wilms tumour, but are less commonly observed. Diagnosis of Wilms tumour typically involves imaging studies, such as an ultrasound or CT scan of the abdomen, which can identify the presence of a mass in the kidney. A biopsy may be performed to confirm the diagnosis, but it is not always necessary. Treatment usually involves surgical resection of the tumour, followed by chemotherapy to reduce the risk of recurrence. Histologically, Wilms tumour is characterized by the presence of blastemal proliferation, which represents the undifferentiated embryonic cells of the kidney. Other histological features of Wilms tumour may include stromal and epithelial components and mesenchymal differentiation. However, papillary architecture, glandular differentiation, squamous differentiation, and neuroendocrine differentiation are not characteristic findings of Wilm's tumour. Incorrect options: Option A. However, it is not a characteristic finding of Wilms tumour. Option E. questions.stem: A 60-year-old man is hospitalized with shortness of breath and leg swelling. He has a medical history of hypertension, type 2 diabetes and recurrent episodes of bilateral flank pain over the past several years. On physical examination, his blood pressure is 165/100 mm Hg. Laboratory tests reveal an elevated serum creatinine level of 3.0 mg/dL and decreased urine output. CT scan of the abdomen is shown in the image below. Which of the following is the likely cause of these findings?
questions.stemHtml: A 60-year-old man is hospitalized with shortness of breath and leg swelling. He has a medical history of hypertension, type 2 diabetes and recurrent episodes of bilateral flank pain over the past several years. On physical examination, his blood pressure is 165/100 mm Hg. Laboratory tests reveal an elevated serum creatinine level of 3.0 mg/dL and decreased urine output. CT scan of the abdomen is shown in the image below. Which of the following is the likely cause of these findings?
questions.solution: Correct Option D: Polycystic kidney disease This man, presenting with acute renal failure with a history of flank pain and hypertension, most likely has autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD). Polycystic kidney disease (PKD) is a genetic disorder in which numerous cysts form in the kidneys, causing them to enlarge and lose function over time. It is called "polycystic" because the cysts develop in clusters, and "kidney disease". After all, it primarily affects the kidneys. There are two main types of PKD: Autosomal dominant PKD (ADPKD) ADPKD is the most common form and is usually diagnosed in adults. A genetic mutation in the PKD1 or PKD2 gene causes it. Autosomal recessive PKD (ARPKD) ARPKD is a rarer form that typically affects infants and children. A mutation in the PKHD1 gene causes it. Symptoms of PKD can include: Back or flank pain Hematuria Frequent urination High blood pressure Nephrolithiasis As the disease progresses, it can lead to kidney failure, which may require dialysis or a kidney transplant. Renal failure occurs in PCKD from recurrent episodes of pyelonephritis and nephrolithiasis, causing progressive scarring and loss of renal function. PCKD does not have malignant potential. Only 10% to 15% of affected people have cerebral aneurysms, most of which do not rupture. Renal failure is the most common complication of PCKD. ADPKD is one of the most common hereditary diseases, accounting for 10% of dialysis patients. Patients will often have hypertension and palpable kidneys on examination. It may be associated with the following: Mitral valve prolapse Benign hepatic cysts Diverticulosis CT scan shows multiple bilateral cysts throughout the renal parenchyma and renal enlargement, consistent with polycystic kidney disease. Incorrect options: Option A: Renal Cyst A renal cyst is a fluid-filled sac that develops within the kidney. It is a common condition that usually does not cause symptoms and is often found incidentally during imaging studies such as ultrasound, CT scan or MRI. Renal cysts can occur in one or both kidneys and range from very small to several centimeters. Most renal cysts are simple cysts, which are benign and do not require any treatment. However, in rare cases, complex renal cysts can develop with solid components or irregularities in their shape or size. These types of cysts may require further evaluation to rule out the possibility of kidney cancer. Renal cysts do not cause symptoms unless they become large enough to compress surrounding structures, such as the ureter or renal pelvis. In such cases, symptoms may include pain in the abdomen or flank, difficulty urinating, or blood in the urine. This patient's CT scan shows multiple cysts and an enlarged renal parenchyma that is specific for polycystic kidney disease. Option B: Medullary sponge kidney Medullary sponge kidney (MSK) is a congenital disorder of the kidneys in which the renal tubules in the medulla, the inner part of the kidney, are dilated and form multiple cysts or cavities. It can be caused by autosomal dominant mutations in the MCKD1 or MCKD2 genes on chromosomes 1 and 16, respectively. It can cause the kidneys to appear spongy when viewed in imaging studies such as ultrasound or CT scans. MSK is usually asymptomatic, and many people with the condition may not know they have it. However, in some cases, MSK can cause urinary tract infections, kidney stones, and recurrent episodes of hematuria (blood in the urine). The dilated tubules can also cause the kidneys to have reduced function. In MSK, the cysts are located in the medulla of the kidney, while in PKD, the cysts are located throughout the kidney, including the cortex and medulla. It is an inherited disease causing tubulointerstitial fibrosis and progressive renal insufficiency with the inability to concentrate urine. Medullary cysts are usually not visualized. They may show shrunken kidneys on ultrasound. CT scan of MSK shows cystic dilatation of the distal collecting tubules, a striated appearance in this area, and calcifications in the renal collecting system. Option C: Renal cell carcinoma Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) is a type of kidney cancer that develops in the cells lining the small tubes within the kidney. RCC is the most common type of kidney cancer in adults, accounting for about 90% of cases. Certain risk factors have been identified, including; Smoking High blood pressure A family history of kidney cancer Symptoms of RCC may include: Hematuria Flank pain Weight loss Fatigue Fever Renal cell carcinoma does not occur with increased frequency in patients with ADPKD compared to the general population. Also, it is less likely given no other symptoms such as weight loss or loss of appetite. RCC alone would not give renal failure. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option A- Goodpasture syndrome: Goodpasture syndrome is an autoimmune disease in which the antibodies attack the basement membranes of the lungs and kidneys. The pathophysiology of Goodpasture syndrome is the formation of autoantibodies against the alpha-3 chain of type-IV collagen in the basement membrane. The immunofluorescence will show the linear deposit of the IgG along the GBM. It can present initially with rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and acute renal failure. It can also involve the lung and can result in haemoptysis. The investigations done in the evaluation and assessment of Goodpasture syndrome are complete blood count, renal function tests, urinalysis, chest x-ray, pulmonary function tests, and immunofluorescence. The investigation of choice for the diagnosis of Goodpasture syndrome is kidney biopsy. Incorrect Options: Option B- Wegener's granulomatosis: Wegener's granulomatosis is an autoimmune condition that involves multiple organs, upper and lower respiratory tract, necrotizing glomerulonephritis, and vasculitis. This condition is positive with anti-nuclear cytoplasmic antibodies against proteinase-3 (PR3-ANCA), which is highly specific for Wegener's granulomatosis. Some of the symptoms are nosebleeds, sinus infections, shortness of breath, coughing, blood in urine, skin rashes, fever, weight loss, etc. Option C- Microscopic polyangiitis: Microscopic polyangiitis is an autoimmune disorder that causes vasculitis and can involve kidneys, lungs, nerves, skin, and joints. Some of the symptoms of microscopic polyangiitis are fever, rashes, and muscle and joint pain. Other symptoms can be shortness of breath, hemoptysis, blood in urine, and swelling of the body. The anti-nuclear cytoplasmic antibodies against myeloperoxidase (MPO-ANCA) are positive in this condition. Option D- Minimal change of disease: Minimal change disease is a nephrotic disease in which there is a loss of protein through the kidneys resulting in decreased serum proteins, increased blood cholesterol and triglycerides. This results in edema in children. This condition is common in children. Some of the causes of minimal change disease are allergies, infections, tumors, drugs, etc. This patient is not suffering from minimal change disease as the symptoms are consistent with the diagnosis of Goodpasture syndrome. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man presented in the ER with a complaint of muscle weakness, and increased heart rate for the past 7 days. Investigation revealed serum bicarbonate:14 mmol/L, Anion Gap is normal. Urine analysis shows no cast, pus cells, or crystals but the pH of urine is 5.2. A diagnosis of renal tubular acidosis type II is suspected. Which part of the nephron is most likely to be involved in the above-mentioned condition?
questions.stemHtml: A 40-year-old man presented in the ER with a complaint of muscle weakness, and increased heart rate for the past 7 days. Investigation revealed serum bicarbonate:14 mmol/L, Anion Gap is normal. Urine analysis shows no cast, pus cells, or crystals but the pH of urine is 5.2. A diagnosis of renal tubular acidosis type II is suspected. Which part of the nephron is most likely to be involved in the above-mentioned condition?
questions.solution: Correct Option C: Proximal convoluted tubule A renal tubular acidosis is a group of diseases that results in the inability of the kidneys to excrete acids out of the blood into the urine. As a result of it, metabolic acidosis results. In Renal tubular acidosis type 2, the proximal convoluted tubule is involved which results in the inability to reabsorb the bicarbonate ions leading to metabolic acidosis. However, the distal tubules are working normally and can acidify the urine. That is why metabolic acidosis is less severe. Hypokalemia is also associated with renal tubular acidosis. Some of the symptoms of renal tubular acidosis type 2 are palpitations, irregular heartbeats, paralysis, and death. In RTA type 2, there are low levels of potassium and bicarbonate. Incorrect options: Option A: Early distal tubule The early distal tubule is affected in renal tubular acidosis type 1, in which there is an inability to excrete acid from the body. It can be inherited from parents or it can be associated with autoimmune conditions like systemic lupus erythematosus, lupus, etc. Renal tubular acidosis type 1 patients are prone to kidney stones. Option B: Capillaries In renal tubular acidosis, capillaries are not the cause of metabolic acidosis. Capillaries surround the nephrons and are involved in providing the blood supply and also reabsorb the molecules so that they can be recirculated in the blood. The obstruction of the capillaries can lead to acute kidney injury. Option D: Collecting duct The collecting duct is the last part of the nephron which reabsorbs the water and electrolytes to concentrate the urine. It also excretes waste materials. The collecting duct is mainly controlled by ADH and aldosterone. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 50-year-old male patient presented in the outpatient department with complaints of fatigue and muscle weakness. The laboratory results revealed low pH, decreased bicarbonate ions, and high potassium. A diagnosis of renal tubular acidosis type 4 is made. Which of the following is the cause of the above-mentioned patient's condition?
questions.stemHtml: A 50-year-old male patient presented in the outpatient department with complaints of fatigue and muscle weakness. The laboratory results revealed low pH, decreased bicarbonate ions, and high potassium. A diagnosis of renal tubular acidosis type 4 is made. Which of the following is the cause of the above-mentioned patient's condition?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Hypoaldosteronism: Hypoaldosteronism is a condition in which there is a deficiency of aldosterone. Normally the activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system leads to the activation of aldosterone. The collecting duct of the nephron is the main site where the aldosterone acts. Normally aldosterone causes the excretion of hydrogen and potassium ions. However, in renal tubular acidosis type 4, there is a deficiency of aldosterone or aldosterone resistance, which results in hyperkalemia. Hyperkalemia can be fatal to the heart and can result in life-threatening arrhythmias. With hyperkalemia, ECG changes can occur. Incorrect Options: Option A - Hyperaldosteronism: Hyperaldosteronism is the excessive aldosterone production that results in excessive excretion of potassium and hydrogen ions. As a result, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis is seen in such patients. Option C - ADH deficiency: Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) acts on vasopressin receptors that cause the expression of receptors in the distal part of nephrons causing the reabsorption of water. In ADH deficiency, there is insufficient ADH which results in excessive excretion of water leading to decreased urine osmolality and high serum osmolarity. Option D - SIADH: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone is a condition in which there is excessive retention of water due to excess ADH. The urine osmolality is high and there is hypervolemia. Some of the causes of SIADH are meningitis, encephalitis, brain tumors, psychosis, lung disease, etc. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option B: Normal anion gap Renal tubular acidosis is due to the inability of the kidney to either excrete hydrogen ions or reabsorb filtered bicarbonate. There are many types of RTA including type 1 RTA, type 2 RTA, and type 4 RTA. Type 1 RTA is due to the inability of the distal tubule of the nephron to excrete hydrogen ions leading to metabolic acidosis. Causes of RTA include primary causes: familial, and idiopathic. Secondary causes include sickle cell anemia, autoimmune (SLE, Sjogren's), hyperparathyroidism, and Vitamin D intoxication, chronic hepatitis, renal transplantation. Anion Gap is used to find the cause of metabolic acidosis. The normal value of the anion gap is 8 to 12 mEq/L. Normal anion gap with metabolic acidosis is due to loss of bicarbonate by the kidney( RTA type 1 and RTA type 2) or gut (Diarrhea). Symptoms include increased respiratory rate, irregular heart rate, muscle weakness, lethargy, constipation, nephrocalcinosis, paralysis, and death. There will be hyperkalemia due to hyperaldosteronism. Incorrect options: Option A: High anion gap metabolic acidosis Conditions with Metabolic acidosis associated with high anion gap include methanol, uremia, diabetic ketoacidosis, paracetamol, paraldehyde, isoniazid, lactic acidosis, ethylene glycol, salicylates etc. (MUDPILES). Option C: Decreased anion gap metabolic acidosis Though not related to acid-base balance, it could signal disease. Conditions with abnormally low anion gap include low serum albumin, increased chloride, hyperkalemia, hypercalcemia, and multiple myeloma. Option D: Metabolic alkalosis Metabolic alkalosis results when there is an increase in bicarbonate ions or a decrease in hydrogen ions. In renal tubular acidosis, there is metabolic acidosis. Some of the causes of metabolic alkalosis are vomiting, diuretics, and hyperaldosteronism. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 36-year-male presented in the hospital ER with a presenting complaint of lethargy, muscle weakness and pain, abdominal pain and constipation. On examination, heart rate: 98/min, respiratory rate:26/min, B.P:100/70 mmHg. Laboratory findings include serum sodium:140 mmol/L, serum potassium:3.2 mmol/L, serum bicarbonate:12 bicarbonate. Arterial blood gas shows pH:7.23. The anion gap is normal. Urine analysis shows pH:5.2, no cast, no RBCs, no protein. Renal tubular acidosis is suspected. What is the buffering mechanism in the kidney to correct acid-base disturbance in this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 36-year-male presented in the hospital ER with a presenting complaint of lethargy, muscle weakness and pain, abdominal pain and constipation. On examination, heart rate: 98/min, respiratory rate:26/min, B.P:100/70 mmHg. Laboratory findings include serum sodium:140 mmol/L, serum potassium:3.2 mmol/L, serum bicarbonate:12 bicarbonate. Arterial blood gas shows pH:7.23. The anion gap is normal. Urine analysis shows pH:5.2, no cast, no RBCs, no protein. Renal tubular acidosis is suspected. What is the buffering mechanism in the kidney to correct acid-base disturbance in this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option B: Phosphate and ammonia buffer system Buffers in the body resist change in the acid-base balance after the addition of either acid or base. There are many types of buffering systems in the body including bicarbonate buffer, hemoglobin buffer, protein buffer etc. The major buffering mechanism in the kidney is the phosphate buffer system and ammonia buffer system. Phosphate buffer is the first line buffering mechanism in the kidney which is freely filtered as mono hydrogen phosphate and is not completely reabsorbed. Monohydrogen phosphate reacts with excess hydrogen ions excreted by the distal tubule of the nephron and forms dihydrogen phosphate. Ammonia buffer is the second line buffering mechanism of the kidney. This ammonia is derived from glutamine in the kidney. Ammonia reacts with excess hydrogen ions and forms ammonium ions. Hydrogen ions in the urine are in 2 forms, dihydrogen phosphate (titratable acid) and ammonium (non-titratable acid). Incorrect options: Option A: Protein Buffer system Protein acts as a buffer in both cells and plasma. Protein is made up of amino acids(A.A). The exposed amine group of A. A accepts hydrogen ions in acidic conditions. The exposed carboxyl group of A. A releases hydrogen ions when there is alkalosis and helps to cancel out its effect. Proteins are not part of the buffering system of the kidney. Option C: Hemoglobin buffer system The Hemoglobin buffer system is the type of protein buffer system inside the RBCs. Hemoglobin is made up of amino acids. Hemoglobin can release and accept hydrogen ions if the condition is alkalotic and acidotic, respectively. Option D: Bicarbonate buffer system The major buffer system in the blood is the bicarbonate buffer system. Carbon dioxide from tissues is converted in RBCs into bicarbonate via the action of carbonic anhydrase and is released back into the plasma. When excess hydrogen ions enter the body, hydrogen ions get neutralized by reacting with bicarbonate forming carbonic acid which dissociates into water and carbon dioxide. Carbon dioxide is carried to the lungs and is exhaled. In this way, bicarbonate prevents change in the pH of the blood. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: A 60-year-old male patient presented in the outpatient department with complaints of nausea, confusion, and decreased urine output for the last 2 weeks. He has a history of long-term uncontrolled hypertension. The laboratory results showed increased anion gap metabolic acidosis. After an appropriate workup, a diagnosis of renal failure is made. Which of the following is the underlying acidosis in this patient's condition?
questions.solution: Correct Option B: Accumulation of organic acids Kidneys are the vital organs of the human body that play an important role in the filtration of blood and excretion of metabolic wastes. Kidneys also produce important hormones like vitamin D, erythropoietin, etc. This patient is suffering from metabolic acidosis with an increased anion gap. This metabolic acidosis results from the accumulation of organic acids in the body. Some of the causes of renal failure are diabetes, high blood pressure, chronic NSAID users, etc. The accumulation of organic acids is the main reason for the increased anion gap. Some of the symptoms of kidney failure are decreased urine output, fatigue, muscle cramps, fluid overload, nausea, vomiting, dry skin, etc. Incorrect options: Option A: Ketones accumulation Ketone accumulation can also result in an increased anion gap metabolic acidosis but in renal failure, the main cause of metabolic acidosis is the accumulation of organic acids. Ketones are accumulated in the body in diabetes. It is a common condition in type I diabetes mellitus in which insulin is deficient. Option C: Accumulation of salicylates Aspirin is usually used for its analgesic and antiplatelet effect for the management of different diseases. The aspirin is also called salicylates. The salicylate overdose can result in metabolic acidosis with an increased anion gap but in renal failure, the main cause of metabolic acidosis is the accumulation of organic acids. It can also cause respiratory alkalosis initially because of the increased respiratory drive. Option D: Accumulation of formate Methanol is an alcohol that is used in antifreeze, perfumes, carburetor cleaners, etc. Methanol toxicity occurs because of unintentional ingestion of methanol. The methanol is converted into formaldehyde by alcohol dehydrogenase. The formaldehyde is further converted into formate by the aldehyde dehydrogenase. It can also cause increased anion gap metabolic acidosis. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option B: Defective beta globin chain Sickle cell disease is an autosomal recessive disease. There is a defect in the beta-globin chain due to the point mutation at position 6 of the beta chain which replaces glutamic acid with valine. Defective beta chains in hemoglobin make RBCs susceptible to sickling in the condition of hypoxia, dehydration and acidosis. Sickled RBCs are irregular in shape and stuck in small blood vessels resulting in vaso-occlusive crisis and hemolysis. Symptoms of sickle cell disease include pallor, jaundice, episodes of pain, swelling of hands and feet, recurrent infections, growth retardation, vision the problem, auto splenectomy (due to infarction). Sickle cell disease is also one of the causes of renal tubular acidosis type 1. Peripheral smear shows target cells and sickled RBCs. Incorrect options: Option A: Decrease synthesis of the beta-globin chain. Beta thalassemia is due to decreased production of the beta globin chain. 2 major types of beta thalassemia include: Beta thalassemia minor which is usually asymptomatic Beta thalassemia major which is symptomatic and manifest after 6 months of life. Symptoms of Beta thalassemia include fatigue, lethargy, pallor, growth retardation, recurrent infections, bony abnormalities (haemolytic facies), enlarged spleen and liver. Blood smear shows hypochromic and microcytic cells with anisocytosis and poikilocytosis Option C: Defect in the utilization of iron during erythropoiesis. Sideroblastic anemia is a type of anemia in which iron is present but iron cannot be incorporated in heme. Iron starts to accumulate inside the mitochondria of RBCs and form a ring around the nucleus such RBCs are called sideroblast. Peripheral smears show microcytic and hypochromic cells with Pappenheimer granules. Option D: Defect in membrane proteins of RBCs. Hereditary spherocytosis is a condition characterized by hemolytic anemia in which there is a defect in the RBCs membrane proteins called ankyrin, Spectrin, and band 3 proteins. Defective RBCs are susceptible to hemolysis. Symptoms include pallor, jaundice, fatigue, lethargy, gallstones, and splenomegaly. Peripheral blood smear shows spherocytes. The Osmotic fragility test is positive. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 12-year-old male patient was brought to the clinic with the complaint of headaches for the past 1 month. There was no associated nausea, vomiting, vision loss, or any other neurological defect. The blood pH revealed a pH of 7.49 (alkalosis) The urinalysis was normal, and the CT scan revealed a small tumor in the right kidney. The renin and aldosterone levels were raised. Which of the following is the underlying cause of hypertension in this patient's condition?
questions.stemHtml: A 12-year-old male patient was brought to the clinic with the complaint of headaches for the past 1 month. There was no associated nausea, vomiting, vision loss, or any other neurological defect. The blood pH revealed a pH of 7.49 (alkalosis) The urinalysis was normal, and the CT scan revealed a small tumor in the right kidney. The renin and aldosterone levels were raised. Which of the following is the underlying cause of hypertension in this patient's condition?
questions.solution: Correct Option B: Reninoma Reninoma is a tumor that is also called juxtaglomerular cell tumor which is characterized by the excessive production of renin. As a result of it, the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system is activated resulting in the retention of the salt and water. It presents mainly with the symptoms of headache due to hypertension. Lethargy, intermittent polyuria and polydipsia can occur in this condition. The heart examination will be normal. There will be no radio-femoral delay. Urinalysis will be normal. Fundoscopy will also be normal. The renin levels will be raised which will cause a rise in the aldosterone levels. The raised aldosterone will result in metabolic alkalosis CT scan will reveal a mass in the kidney. The treatment of the reninoma is the removal of the tumor which will remove the source of production of renin. Incorrect options: Option A: Cushing disease Cushing disease is the excessive production of cortisol by the adrenal gland which results in obesity, a moon-shaped face, hypertension, striae, humped back, diabetes, etc. However, Cushing disease will not result in high renin and aldosterone levels. However, the raised levels of cortisol will directly result in hypertension. Option C: Excess aldosterone production Excessive aldosterone can also present with metabolic alkalosis, hypokalaemia, and hypertension. However, in the excess of aldosterone, there is negative feedback leading to a decrease in renin production. Whereas in this patient, the raised aldosterone level is caused by the raised renin levels. Option D: Renal artery stenosis Renal artery stenosis can also cause uncontrolled hypertension that is resistant to drugs. The decreased blood supply due to renal artery stenosis results in the activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system. However, in this patient, the CT scan revealed a mass in the right kidney which is consistent with the diagnosis of the reninoma. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes presents with nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. Labs reveal blood glucose of 460 mg/dL, pH of 7.20, and potassium of 2.2 mEq/L. Urinalysis is positive for ketones. What is the most appropriate initial intervention?
questions.stemHtml: A 32-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes presents with nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. Labs reveal blood glucose of 460 mg/dL, pH of 7.20, and potassium of 2.2 mEq/L. Urinalysis is positive for ketones. What is the most appropriate initial intervention?
questions.solution: Correct Option A. Administer 0.45% NaCl infusion: This is the correct initial intervention. The patient is presenting with diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), which is characterized by hyperglycemia, ketosis, and metabolic acidosis. The low blood pH (7.20) indicates acidosis. The patient's low potassium level (2.2 mEq/L) suggests hypokalemia, likely due to intracellular shifts of potassium as a result of acidosis. Administering a 0.45% NaCl (normal saline) infusion helps to correct dehydration, electrolyte imbalances, and acidosis. It also assists in improving tissue perfusion. After initiating fluid resuscitation, insulin administration can be started to help lower blood glucose levels and further correct acidosis Incorrect options: Option B. Administer potassium chloride: While hypokalemia (low potassium) is a potential complication of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), administering potassium chloride as the initial intervention can be dangerous. The patient's potassium level is already low (2.2 mEq/L), and administering potassium without proper fluid resuscitation can lead to further imbalances and potentially life-threatening cardiac arrhythmias. Correcting fluid balance is the priority before addressing potassium imbalances. Option C. Administer 0.1 units/kg IV insulin: While insulin administration is a crucial component of DKA treatment, it should not be the initial step in this case. Before insulin is administered, it's important to address the patient's fluid and electrolyte imbalances. Administering insulin without adequate hydration can lead to further decreases in potassium levels and potential complications. Option D. Administer a dextrose solution: Administering a dextrose solution is not appropriate as the initial intervention for DKA. The patient's blood glucose level is already very high (460 mg/dL), and giving more glucose can exacerbate the hyperglycemia and worsen the acidosis. The primary concern in DKA management is first addressing fluid and electrolyte imbalances. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 28-year-old male presents with a headache, nausea, vomiting, and dizziness after climbing to an altitude of 12,000 feet. Physical examination reveals an unsteady gait, and the patient is diagnosed with mountain sickness. Which of the following diuretics is most useful in the management of mountain sickness?
questions.stemHtml: A 28-year-old male presents with a headache, nausea, vomiting, and dizziness after climbing to an altitude of 12,000 feet. Physical examination reveals an unsteady gait, and the patient is diagnosed with mountain sickness. Which of the following diuretics is most useful in the management of mountain sickness?
questions.solution: Correct Option A: Acetazolamide Acetazolamide is a diuretic that primarily acts in the proximal tubules of the kidney to inhibit the enzyme carbonic anhydrase . Carbonic anhydrase catalyzes the reversible reaction between water and carbon dioxide to form bicarbonate and a hydrogen ion . Inhibition of this enzyme by acetazolamide leads to decreased bicarbonate reabsorption in the proximal tubules , which in turn leads to increased excretion of bicarbonate and a reduction in the reabsorption of sodium and water . When individuals ascend to high altitudes, there is a decrease in the partial pressure of oxygen in the atmosphere, which can lead to hypoxia (low oxygen levels) and an increase in carbon dioxide retention . As a result, the body attempts to compensate for this by increasing respiratory rate, heart rate and by increasing bicarbonate reabsorption in the kidneys. Acetazolamide , by inhibiting carbonic anhydrase, can counteract this compensation mechanism by causing an increase in the excretion of bicarbonate, leading to metabolic acidosis . This metabolic acidosis stimulates the respiratory centre in the brain to increase ventilation , which helps to alleviate the symptoms of mountain sickness. In addition, acetazolamide can also cause an increase in urine output , which can help to reduce fluid retention and oedema that can occur at high altitudes . Therefore, acetazolamide is the diuretic of choice in the management of mountain sickness. Incorrect options: Option B: Furosemide Furosemide is a loop diuretic that works in the ascending limb of the loop of Henle in the kidney to inhibit sodium and chloride reabsorption . While furosemide can be an effective treatment for conditions such as oedema and hypertension, it is not typically used in the management of mountain sickness. One reason is that furosemide does not address the underlying cause of mountain sickness , which is a decrease in the partial pressure of oxygen at high altitudes. In contrast, acetazolamide alleviates mountain sickness symptoms by increasing respiratory drive and reducing fluid retention , which helps compensate for the low oxygen levels at high altitudes. Additionally, using furosemide to manage mountain sickness may be counterproductive, as it can lead to dehydration and electrolyte imbalances . This can exacerbate nausea, headache and fatigue associated with mountain sickness. Option C: Hydrochlorothiazide Hydrochlorothiazide is a thiazide diuretic that acts on the distal tubules of the nephron to block the activity of the Na+/Cl- symporter , which normally allows these ions to be reabsorbed into the bloodstream. As a result, sodium and chloride ions are excreted in the urine, leading to increased water excretion. One of the potential side effects of hydrochlorothiazide is metabolic alkalosis , which can occur due to the loss of hydrogen ions in the urine. This can lead to an increase in blood pH and a decrease in bicarbonate ion concentration . Therefore, hydrochlorothiazide would not be effective for the management of mountain sickness as it could potentiate the metabolic alkalosis already present . Instead, treatment for mountain sickness typically involves oxygen therapy, descent to lower altitudes, and the use of medications such as acetazolamide, which can help alleviate symptoms by increasing respiratory drive and reducing the risk of cerebral oedema. Option D: Spironolactone Spironolactone is a potassium-sparing diuretic which acts on the late distal tubule and cortical collecting ducts and prevents the aldosterone-mediated exchange of sodium and potassium ions, leading to increased excretion of sodium and decreased excretion of potassium ions. Spironolactone does not affect acid-base balance directly , and hence, it’s not typically used for the management of mountain sickness. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old male presents to the emergency department with a history of a fall from a ladder. He complains of difficulty breathing and exhibits signs of respiratory distress. On examination, you suspect a cervical spine injury. Which of the following airway maneuvers should be avoided in this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Head tilt/Chin lift: In a patient with suspected cervical spine injury, the head tilt/chin lift maneuver should be avoided. This maneuver involves placing the dominant hand on the patient's forehead and tilting the head down while using the index and middle fingers of the other hand to lift the chin. It is designed to open the airway by extending the neck. However, it cannot be safely performed in patients with suspected cervical spine injury due to the risk of exacerbating the injury. Incorrect Options: Option B - Jaw thrust: Jaw thrust is the recommended maneuver for patients with suspected cervical spine injury. It involves manipulating the angle of the mandible to open the airway without moving the cervical spine. Option C - Oropharyngeal airway and Option D - Nasopharyngeal airway are both basic airway devices used for airway management. While oropharyngeal airways may induce a gag reflex and are preferred in patients with a low Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS), nasopharyngeal airways are softer tubes that do not induce a gag reflex and are used in patients with a good GCS. These devices do not involve movement of the cervical spine. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option C - Administer a neuromuscular blocking agent, perform laryngoscopy and endotracheal intubation, then administer sedative and analgesic agents: Rapid sequence intubation (RSI) is a technique used to secure the airway in critically ill patients while minimizing the risk of aspiration. The correct sequence of actions during RSI is as follows: Administer a neuromuscular blocking agent (NMBA): The first step in RSI is to administer a rapid-acting NMBA, such as succinylcholine or rocuronium. This paralyzes the patient's muscles, including the vocal cords, and prevents them from resisting or coughing during intubation. Perform laryngoscopy and endotracheal intubation: After the NMBA has been administered and the patient is paralyzed, the healthcare provider performs laryngoscopy to visualize the vocal cords and then proceeds with endotracheal intubation to secure the airway. This step should be performed as quickly as possible to minimize the risk of hypoxia. Administer sedative and analgesic agents: Once the endotracheal tube is in place and the airway is secured, sedative and analgesic agents, such as propofol or etomidate (sedative) and fentanyl or midazolam (analgesic), are administered to achieve deep sedation and prevent discomfort or awareness in the patient. The correct sequence is crucial in RSI to ensure a smooth and safe intubation process while minimizing the risk of complications, such as aspiration or patient discomfort. Incorrect Options: Options A, B, and D are incorrect because they do not follow the recommended sequence of RSI. Administering sedative and analgesic agents before paralyzing the patient's muscles can lead to coughing, gagging, or resistance during intubation, increasing the risk of complications. @Neet_pg_bot

    • Administer sedative and analgesic agents: Once the endotracheal tube is in place and the airway is secured, sedative and analgesic agents, such as propofol or etomidate (sedative) and fentanyl or midazolam (analgesic), are administered to achieve deep sedation and prevent discomfort or awareness in the patient.

options.label: A
options.text: Drain the paronychia with a blunt instrument and then drain the felon with a longitudinal midline incision on the pulp space, extending through and through. Discharge on antibiotics

options.label: B
options.text: This is a significant infection. It needs a hand surgeon immediately. Transfer him to the ER

options.label: C
options.text: Drain the paronychia but do not pack it. Discharge the patient with warm soaks for several days.

questions.solution: Correct Option A - Drain the paronychia with a blunt instrument and then drain the felon with a longitudinal midline incision on the pulp space, extending through and through. Discharge on antibiotics: This is a paronychia and felon and should be drained. The technique to drain this is important . A fishmouth incision should be avoided . The paronychia can be drained with a blunt instrument along the lateral nail bed and opened up to allow drainage. The felon (pulp space infection) needs to be drained separately and a palmar midline incision should be made into the pulp space. This can be extended through and through and then packed with gauze. A horizontal incision is not recommended as the tendon can be cut or the infection spread into the tendon sheath, potentially making things worse. questions.solution: Correct Option A – Hypocalcemia: Patient’s symptoms are concerning for hypocalcemia, which this patient is most at risk for after a three-and-a-half-gland parathyroidectomy. Incorrect Options: Option B - Hypovitaminosis D : This patient’s vitamin D is most likely low from his renal failure. Patients with renal insufficiency have impaired 1,25 (OH)2 D production. However, vitals are stable, and symptoms are not consistent with low hemoglobin. Option D - Hypovitaminosis of B 12 : Low vitamin B 12 may cause neuropathy but not a positive Chovstek’s sign. The group is exploring a shipwreck around 125 feet below the surface when the man begins to start swimming away from the group despite them motioning for him to stay close by. One of the other divers quickly recognizes the emergency and brings the patient to the surface. What is the most likely cause of this divers behavior?
questions.stemHtml: A 58-year-old man is diving with two other friends in the beach. One of the other divers quickly recognizes the emergency and brings the patient to the surface. What is the most likely cause of this divers behavior?
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Nitrogen narcosis: Nitrogen narcosis is a complication of diving seen at depth of 100 feet of water or greater . It results from increased solubility of nitrogen in the blood stream as pressure increases at depth . Symptoms include loss of fine motor skills and behavior similar to alcohol intoxication . Treatment is controlled ascent. Incorrect Options: Option A - Pulmonary barotrauma : Pulmonary barotrauma occurs during ascent when a diver ascends with a closed glottis. Air in the lungs will expand as pressure decreases with ascent, causing damage to the lungs. Option B - Arterial gas embolism : Arterial gas embolism refers to air in the arterial circulation. It is usually a complication of pulmonary barotrauma and presents with sudden onset neurologic symptoms or cardiovascular collapse. It usually presents during ascent or immediately on surfacing. Treatment is hyperbaric therapy. Option C - Alternobaric vertigo : Alternobaric vertigo occurs when air is trapped in the middle ear canal and expands during ascent, causing unequal vestibular impulses to the brain. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: An 8-year-old girl is admitted through the emergency department with nausea, vomiting, and acidosis. She is diagnosed with diabetic ketoacidosis, but her parents do not want her to be administered insulin or receive IV fluids until they have an opportunity to “do some research on this topic.” The patient is deteriorating clinically, but her parents persist in their refusal even after hearing the consequences of failing to treat the child. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
questions.stemHtml: An 8-year-old girl is admitted through the emergency department with nausea, vomiting, and acidosis. She is diagnosed with diabetic ketoacidosis, but her parents do not want her to be administered insulin or receive IV fluids until they have an opportunity to “do some research on this topic.” The patient is deteriorating clinically, but her parents persist in their refusal even after hearing the consequences of failing to treat the child. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.text: Report the parents to Child Protective Services

options.label: B
options.text: Administer insulin and fluids as indicated

options.label: C
options.text: Do not administer treatment to this patient without parental consent

questions.answerText: Administer insulin and fluids as indicated
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Administer insulin and fluids as indicated: In an emergency that threatens life, limb or eyesight, the health care provider has a duty to treat a minor despite parental refusal. First, the practitioner should attempt to explain and to convince the parents, but if there is a clear and imminent danger to the patient, health care professionals can treat without judicial review. If there is time, the practitioner can obtain a court order to pursue the authority to treat. Incorrect Options: Option A - Report the parents to Child Protective Services: There is no reason to report the parents to CPS unless there are concerns about withholding or delaying necessary medical care. Option C - Do not administer treatment to this patient without parental consent: Consent is not required for emergency care. Option D - Convene an ethics committee: There is insufficient time to seek a court order or convene an ethics committee in this case. @Neet_pg_bot

Incorrect Options:

Option A - Report the parents to Child Protective Services: There is no reason to report the parents to CPS unless there are concerns about withholding or delaying necessary medical care.

Option C - Do not administer treatment to this patient without parental consent: Consent is not required for emergency care.

Option D - Convene an ethics committee: There is insufficient time to seek a court order or convene an ethics committee in this case.
